articles.title: Defense cries foul over prosecution's last minute bid to switch witness
articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte objected to the attempt of the prosecution panel to replace the witness from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) who was scheduled to testify for…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 10:50am

The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte objected to the attempt of the prosecution panel to replace the witness from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) who was scheduled to testify for Thursday’s impeachment trial.

This, after House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list requested that the impeachment court be allowed to present financial analyst Alexander Cabrera first, as lawyer Erwin Matib, the private prosecutor who was supposed to present BIR Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Atty. Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, was supposedly sick.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison, however, argued that the move was “really unfair,” stressing that their team had already prepared for the testimony of the BIR official.

“We object to this switching at the last minute. In fact, not even at the last minute, today of the witness that the prosecution intends to present today. We prepared for the BIR witness which they had disclosed. Had they known that problem since yesterday, we expect that we would have at least been notified yesterday, Your Honor,” Sison said.
“We don’t know if this belated notice, ultra belated notice, will suffice to afford the respondent the opportunity to prepare for their supposed forensic financial analyst,” she added.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero noted that the impeachment court has not yet issued a subpoena for Cabrera, but Ridon said that the financial analyst is already in the holding room in the chamber. —AOL,GMA News

articles.title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.summary:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage

Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.

Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”

Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.

In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.

“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America,” and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”

The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/ Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.

Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.

Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.

Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”

The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of Republican governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.

Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title: La Salle banks on Jacob Cortez for past, present, future
articles.summary: With the win, the Green Archers tie the all-time head-to-head record between Ateneo and La Salle at 50-50 after 100 meetings

blocks.text: LEADER. La Salle's Jacob Cortez (second from left) takes charge for the Green Archers.
UAAP
With the win, the Green Archers tie the all-time head-to-head record between Ateneo and La Salle at 50-50 after 100 meetings

items: Jacob Cortez scored 8 of his 12 points in the fourth quarter, leading La Salle to an 83-76 victory over Ateneo in their 100th rivalry game.
Despite a slow start, Cortez's performance helped La Salle tie the all-time series record against Ateneo at 50-50.
Cortez is not only a key player but also a mentor to rookie Joaquin Tovera, who contributed significantly to the game while learning from the veteran.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – In the 100th game of the Ateneo-La Salle rivalry, Jacob Cortez did not look exactly like the star who led the Green Archers to a UAAP championship last year, at least through the first three quarters.
But as usual, Cortez delivered when it mattered most for La Salle.
Cortez scored 8 of his 12 points in the fourth quarter to help the Green Archers overcome the Blue Eagles, 83-76, in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball on Wednesday night, October 7.

“I don’t know if you remember a few weeks ago, he (Cortez) let us lose when we played UST,” said La Salle head coach Topex Robinson, who has steered the Green Archers to back-to-back wins over UE and Ateneo after absorbing a close loss to the Growling Tigers two weeks ago.
“But you have to remember also, several months ago, he won the championship for us.”

La Salle continued to turn to Cortez even after a shaky first three quarters, when he struggled to knock down his usual jumpers and get fruitful drives to the basket. He finished 4-of-13 from the field, along with 3 rebounds, 5 assists, and 2 turnovers.
“He will always take those shots; that’s what he’s built for. We will always win with Jacob. We will lose with Jacob. And that scenario will never change,” Robinson said.
“He always does the right thing. He always disobeys our sets, but he delivers. What’s important, I guess, is that his teammates around him know that he’s gonna take those shots.”

Down by as many as 7 points in the second half, Cortez gave La Salle life, sparking a 31-18 finishing run in the final 15 minutes of the game that allowed the Green Archers to pull away from the Blue Eagles.
The win also tied the all-time head-to-head record between Ateneo and La Salle at 50-50 after 100 meetings.

But Cortez’s value to La Salle extends beyond what he produces on the court as he has also become a mentor to 18-year-old rookie Joaquin Tovera, who held the fort for the Green Archers while the former NCAA and UAAP champion struggled to find his rhythm.
Tovera led La Salle with 15 points on 4-of-8 shooting from the field, along with 4 rebounds and 4 assists in 21 minutes as Cortez’s backup.
“It’s nice for [Tovera] to be with Jacob in his young career. He gets to learn a lot from his kuya (big brother),” Robinson said.

Robinson said Tovera did not fully understand the magnitude of an Ateneo-La Salle game, but that may have helped relieve some of the pressure on the rookie entering what could be their biggest game of the first round.
“This is an 18-year-old kid who doesn’t even know the Ateneo-La Salle rivalry,” he said. “He was just chilling in the dugout. He doesn’t know the gravity of what he’s doing.”
Aside from Tovera, JC Macalalag also scored 15 points and played a crucial role in limiting Ateneo’s prized rookie Kieffer Alas, who finished with just 5 points.
Cortez and Macalalag, who are both playing in their final UAAP seasons, are expected to pass on La Salle’s championship culture into the next generation led by Tovera.
“These two guys are going to be on their final year. We are really making sure that they will have somebody that’s going to follow their lead,” Robinson said.
For now, Robinson is reminding Tovera that he is playing for a special squad led by a championship-caliber veteran in Cortez.
“I just remind [Tovera] all the time that you’re going to look back at this and tell yourself how blessed and fortunate you are to be a part of this team.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: IMF reaches tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal with Pakistan
articles.summary: Pakistan's dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing has left the economy exposed to the fallout from the Middle East conflict.

image.caption: Pakistan has seen soaring prices in recent months that threatened an already fragile economy [FILE: July 16, 2019]Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that could unlock about $1.21 billion (roughly €1 billion) in financing, the lender said on Wednesday, as the South Asian country grapples with spiking food and fuel prices, and high unemployment.
The bailout deal still needs to be approved by the IMF Executive Board.
IMF negotiator Iva Petrova said Pakistan had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict, with strong policies helping preserve macroeconomic stability.
How does the Middle East conflict impact Pakistan?
Pakistan's economy grew 4% in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 with full-year growth estimated at 3.6%, the IMF said.
Petrova attributed the weakened momentum to "higher energy prices and supply disruptions."
Inflation eased to about 10.3% in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, Petrova said.
Pakistan remains dependent on external financing to shore up foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

A prolonged Middle East conflict makes it particularly vulnerable due to its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing from the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Ahmad Mobeen earlier this year.
In the recent past, Pakistan has had to turn to the IMF to tackle Islamabad's acute balance-of-payments crisis.

articles.title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Revelation comes after company’s executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message

  • Get our

blocks.text: OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.

Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.
OpenAI was contacted for comment.

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.
The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.

OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.

Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.
During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.

“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.
Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”

Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.

The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.

“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”

The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.

“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.
after newsletter promotion
“Best, OpenAI Security Team.”

Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.
“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.
“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”
Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.

The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.
“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.
“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”

articles.title: [Good Business] The AI nutrition label: Why we need to know what’s inside before we trust it
articles.summary: When we buy food, we read the label to understand its ingredients, nutritional value, and expiration date. We should apply the same principle to AI.

items: The integration of AI into various sectors raises fundamental questions about trust, transparency, and explainability, emphasizing the need for clarity in AI decision-making processes.
Trustworthy AI requires that organizations be open about how AI systems operate, ensuring that users can understand and question the decisions made by these technologies.
Responsibility for AI outcomes lies with humans, and fostering a culture of transparency and accountability is essential for building trust in AI applications.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Whenever a new artificial intelligence (AI) application is introduced, the first questions are usually practical: What can it do? Will it make work faster? Can it improve productivity, reduce costs, or help us make better decisions?

These questions matter as AI becomes increasingly integrated into our workplaces, schools, businesses, and everyday lives. But before we ask what AI can do for us, perhaps we should first ask a more fundamental question:
Can we trust it?

This question lies at the heart of Transparency and Explainability, one of the eight guiding principles in the Association of Analytics and AI of the Philippines (AAP) Code of Ethics for AI Professionals. It belongs to the pillar of Trustworthy AI, which challenges us to ask a simple but powerful Filipino question:
“Mapagkakatiwalaan ba ito?” (Can this be trusted?)

The question is familiar because we ask it in many areas of life. When we buy food, we read the label to understand its ingredients, nutritional value, and expiration date. When a doctor prescribes medicine, we ask what it is for, how much to take, and what side effects it may have. (READ: Warning labels on food? How a new bill could change Filipino diets)
We do not consume something simply because it is available or because someone says it works. We seek clarity because trust is built on understanding.
We should apply the same principle to AI.

Today, AI helps determine what appears in our social media feeds, what products are recommended to us, and what content we consume. Organizations use it to screen job applicants, assess employees, forecast outcomes, detect fraud, and support decisions. In healthcare, finance, education, and government, AI is increasingly becoming an adviser.
Yet unlike a food label or medicine leaflet, many AI systems remain difficult for ordinary people to understand.

Transparency means being open about when AI is being used, what data it relies on, and its capabilities and limitations. Explainability means that when an AI system makes a recommendation or influences a decision, people can understand the reasoning behind it in language that makes sense.
Simply put:
If AI affects people, people deserve an explanation.
This becomes especially important when AI influences decisions about jobs, promotions, loans, insurance, healthcare, education, or access to opportunities.

Imagine applying for a job and receiving an automated rejection without knowing why. Imagine being denied a loan because of a risk score no one can explain. Or imagine an employee being classified as a low performer by an algorithm, yet neither the employee nor the manager understands how the assessment was made.
The issue is not simply whether AI was used.
The issue is whether people can understand and trust the process behind the decision.

As someone who has spent much of my professional life in human resources, talent analytics, and digital transformation, I find this especially important in the workplace. Organizations are rapidly adopting AI in recruitment, workforce planning, performance management, and talent development. These technologies can improve efficiency and help leaders process information at a scale that would otherwise be impossible.
But efficiency alone should never define success.
People are not data points. Careers are not algorithms. Human potential cannot be fully captured by a score generated by a machine.
When technology begins influencing livelihoods and futures, transparency becomes more than a technical feature. It becomes an ethical responsibility.

blocks.caption: Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

blocks.text: Trust is not created by sophisticated algorithms alone. It grows when people understand how decisions are made, when organizations are willing to explain their systems, and when individuals can question outcomes that affect them.

Transparency also benefits organizations. Employees are more likely to accept AI-assisted processes when they understand them. Customers are more willing to engage with AI-powered services when they know how their information is being used. Regulators, investors, and stakeholders gain confidence when organizations can explain and justify the technologies they deploy.
In this sense, transparency is not merely an ethical requirement. It is also a business advantage.
This is why responsibility belongs to everyone in the AI ecosystem.

For users, it means asking questions instead of accepting every AI-generated recommendation at face value. We need to understand when AI is being used, recognize its limitations, and verify important outputs.

For developers and designers, it means building understandable systems, documenting how they work, testing for unintended consequences, and communicating limitations honestly. Innovation should never come at the expense of clarity.
For leaders, it means establishing governance, ensuring meaningful human oversight, and creating environments where AI recommendations can be challenged. Most importantly, leaders must remember:
Accountability cannot be delegated to a machine.
When an AI-assisted decision causes harm, responsibility ultimately rests with the humans who designed, approved, deployed, and relied on the technology.
Ultimately, the future of AI will not be determined only by how powerful the technology becomes. It will also be determined by how responsibly we choose to use it.
The question before us, therefore, is not simply whether AI is intelligent enough.
The more important question is:
Is it trustworthy enough?
Whenever AI influences our decisions, organizations, or communities, we would do well to return to the challenge posed by the AAP Code of Ethics:
If we cannot understand it, explain it, or question it, perhaps we should not trust it just yet.

Because trustworthy AI is ultimately not about machines. It is about people—and our commitment to ensuring that technology remains transparent, accountable, and worthy of the trust we place in it. – Rappler.com

Liza Manalo-Mapagu is the CEO of ASEAMETRICS, Program Chair of the Psychology Department at Asia Pacific College, and a member of the Responsible AI and Analytics Council (RAAIC) of the Association of Analytics and AI of the Philippines (AAP). She advocates for Trustworthy and Human-Centric AI that advances both organizational performance and human dignity.

articles.title: Woman at centre of Cornell gang-rape case was 'misled' about investigation, lawyer says
articles.summary: The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said…

image.caption: Cornell's police department gave the woman at the centre of gang-rape allegations the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, her lawyer says — but the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began. (Matt Burkhartt/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.
Criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began, but Jane Doe was given impression it was ongoing: lawyer

Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.
In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.

items: Allegations in Cornell 7 case fit pattern of institutional failure on sexual assault, says sociologist

blocks.text: Van Houten has said he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.
Giuffra said the woman was told the criminal investigation was ongoing.
"I think she was misled," he said. "I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren't doing anything."
At the time, Giuffra added, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
"But nothing was being done, and we didn't know that," he said.
A messages seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell's media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university's police department.

The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman's account, written by a police officer.
'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know
Different accounts
Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman's participation in drug use and sex was "voluntary, conscious and consensual."

That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.

Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped," that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available.

Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, the New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten's office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.
"At first I thought these police were incompetent," Giuffra said. "It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down."

Giuffra said while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support — including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.
Cornell students protest university handling of sexual assault case
Case taken away from Van Houten

Jane Doe, who was a student in 2024, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several of them sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.

Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.

The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.

items: Jane Doe at centre of Cornell rape case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
Cornell taps ex-Justice Department official Sally Yates to review school's handling of sexual assault cases

blocks.text: Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten's plan for conducting the reopened investigation and "didn't think he was up to the task."
Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.

That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested Van Houten may have been trying "to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation," Giuffra said.
James hasn't said how long her investigation might take, but suggested it could be months.

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James's removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable."
A spokesperson for James declined to comment.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.

This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. deputy attorney general Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.

articles.title: Jurors in Beau Lamarre-Condon murder case shown photos of decomposed bodies
articles.summary:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Photographs of the decomposed bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies have been shown to 15 jurors tasked with deciding whether the two men were murdered.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Baird, 26, and Davies, 29.
The third week of his double murder trial has pivoted to how investigators found the remains in rural NSW.

Retired crime scene officer Greg Moon, who coordinated the forensic sweep of the Greek monastery at Bungonia where the men’s bodies were found, continued giving evidence on Thursday about the condition of the remains.
Most of the family members of Baird, a former TV presenter, and Davies, a Qantas flight attendant, have not been present in court for the grisly forensic evidence.
Justice Natalie Adams warned jurors on Thursday they would see confronting photos of decomposition.
The bodies were discovered inside two surfboard or stand-up paddleboard bags, with the smaller bag containing the body zipped up inside a larger one, Moon said.
Moon said the bodies were discovered one on top of the other with rocks and small branches placed on top.

blocks.caption: Evidence and testimony in week two of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s trial – video

blocks.text: Fellow investigator Christine Abela said she immediately knew something was amiss when she first arrived at the rural property more than a week after the two men were killed in the summer of 2024.
“There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday.
“The scent of a decomposing body.”
Abela detailed how investigators found concrete blocks, a gym weight and a cut padlock at Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly unsuccessfully attempted to sink the bodies in a dam.
after newsletter promotion
Moon said there were multiple indicators that the remains had been at the monastery, about 20km away from the farm, for several days.
“A large number of maggots and other insects were present in the bags along with other decompositional fluids,” he said.
Lamarre-Condon’s efforts to clean up and dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies have come under scrutiny during the trial.
His barrister says the actions to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia, 200km south of Sydney, were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.

Earlier in the trial, jurors were shown CCTV of the alleged actions the senior constable took in the hours after the killings, including buying a second surfboard bag and hiring a larger second vehicle.
The footage, released by the court on Thursday, allegedly shows the heavily disguised Lamarre-Condon returning to the alleged murder scene laden down with cleaning products and a tarpaulin.
The 12-week trial continues.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 7: VP and husband's millions
articles.summary: A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that attest to her and her husband's alleged wealth.

Article II charges Duterte with amassing wealth disproportionate to her lawful income and failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband Manases Carpio’s assets in her SALNs (statements of assets, liabilities and net worth) for 2022, 2023 and 2024.
It also accuses her of failing to divest from businesses, as the Constitution requires of the president and vice president.

In calling the bank and insurance witnesses, the prosecution sought to put on record the year-end balances in the couple’s accounts, so it can compare each year’s balance against the SALN for the same year.
Prosecutors have argued the records are meant to establish a baseline of Duterte’s wealth and a “pattern of non-disclosure.”

The marathon hearing on Wednesday laid out two clashing ways of reading Duterte’s finances. It's the prosecution's argument that there are serious indications of undeclared wealth just by comparing the SALN and bank balances alone. Citing bank records, the prosecution has pointed out that the Duterte couple had P59 million in bank balances at the end of 2022, her first year in office, against P13.325 million in declared “other personal properties.”

The defense, meanwhile, has countered that transactions from before she took office are irrelevant and that not all the transactions being wielded as evidence by the prosecution were signed off by Duterte herself.
Duterte and her husband have more than 30 to 40 total bank accounts across eight different banks, according to the prosecution.
Here are the three highlights from the proceedings on October 7.
1. The ‘tinikling’ manager’s checks

A bank executive told the court that P41.7 million from a time deposit in the names of Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, was repeatedly moved into bank-issued checks in 2011.

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) division head Marvin Galvez testified that the money started as a P40.65-million time deposit opened in January 2010. By March 9, 2011, the amount had matured to P41.72 million after the interest had accumulated during several rollover periods. On this day, the funds were moved to the Dutertes' joint account at BPI’s Julia Vargas branch.

The same day, the full amount was used to buy a manager’s check, a check guaranteed by the bank and valid for six months. After that check lapsed, another for the same amount was bought on Oct. 20, 2011.

Upon questioning, Galvez confirmed that money held in a manager’s check leaves the depositor’s account but does not appear in the year-end balance. Instead, it is moved into the bank's internal settlement account, making it the bank's liability.

Because of this, prosecutors pointed to the checks as a way of bypassing the SALN by keeping the money in limbo, given public officials are required to declare their cash on hand or in bank, among others, when they file the document by the end of each year.
Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said the money moved this way for “three or four years.” He said a second deposit, of P55 million, was handled the same way, bringing the total to P96 million.
Galvez’s records also showed four transfers of P20 million each from the Dutertes' joint account to BPI-Philam Life on March 28, 2014, for insurance plans worth P80 million in total.
A P16.85-million manager’s check from the same account was made out to "Samuel C. Uy" in May 2016, according to documents read out in court.

Sen. Tito Sotto, in his interjection, compared the alleged scheme to tinikling, the folk dance in which dancers dodge clapping bamboo poles. When Sen. Bam Aquino asked if it was a "known practice" among bankers, Galvez said it was “not uncommon” for clients to return unused checks.
Galvez said he could not tell the extent to which clients do it on purpose, but noted that purchasing managers' checks require them to state their reason for doing so in the application form.
Defense counsel Michael Poa claimed Duterte had no knowledge of the BPI joint account she had with her father and was only made aware of it during prior House hearings.

The joint account was also structured in a way that only the elder Duterte could transact alone, Poa pointed out, while Sara Duterte as co-depositor required her father's permission to move around any funds.
Poa also noted that the BPI records presented during the trial, including the P41.7-million manager's check, bore the signature of the former president and not Sara Duterte.
2. Millions in the bank, year after year
Bank witnesses put the couple’s combined year-end balances across eight banks at the following amounts, as summarized by the prosecution:

items: 2022: P59 million
2023: P71.3 million
2024: P22.2 million

blocks.text: On the flip side, the vice president declared zero cash on hand or in the bank for her SALNs from 2022 to 2024.
But the defense has long sought to debunk the allegation that Duterte misdeclared her wealth by explaining that cash on hand was grouped under "others" or "other personal properties" in her SALNs.

Based on the bank records cited by the prosecution, however, the Duterte couple's 2022 year-end balance of P59 million is more than four times the P13.325 million that was declared in “other personal properties” in the SALN that year.
Under cross-examination, the bank witnesses said they had no personal knowledge of the accounts and testified only from records produced under subpoena.

The Duterte couple kept at least 30 active accounts across eight banks from 2022 to 2025: LandBank, AUB, PSBank, Metrobank, Security Bank, BPI, PNB and BDO. These include accounts held jointly with other family members.
At BPI alone, Galvez counted seven active and 34 closed personal accounts, plus two credit card accounts and one corporate account.
3. Did Security Bank flag Cale88 transactions as suspicious?

Security Bank official Leslie Cham testified that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of Carpio, kept two peso checking accounts with the bank. One was opened in August 2024 and the other in October 2025. Both were closed in July 2026, the month the trial began.

Cham said Cale88’s account recorded P40.14 million in inflows and P40 million in outflows in 2024, and P6.27 million in inflows in 2025. The two accounts closed with balances of P332,530.95 and P21,164.27.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then read from suspicious transaction reports on Cale88 as provided by the Anti-Money Laundering Council:

items: There were 12 cash deposits flagged as not matching Cale88 declared financial profile
Cale88 was flagged for failing to provide supporting documents and stopped responding to requests for clarification, so the bank could not verify where the money came from or what it was for.

blocks.text: Asked whether it was Security Bank that filed those reports, Cham said: “I cannot confirm.”
Cham invoked the confidentiality clause of the Anti-Money Laundering Act and said he could not say whether suspicious transaction records were indeed filed on Cale88.

Corporate records identify Cale88 as a Davao-based banana chips exporter. But the prosecution previously raised red flags about the firm, such as its low reported electricity bills, unusual for a food factory, as well as its large inward remittances from Chinese companies.
October 7 was the longest trial day yet, surpassing the previous record holder just two days before, which lasted around nine hours.

articles.summary: Former DPWH official Juliet Calvo, who faces charges over a P289.5-million dike project, will be returned to jail even after suffering a stroke

blocks.text: ‘MANANANGGAL’ PROJECT. Work resumes on a 2022 flood control project in Oriental Mindoro amid the controversy over anomalous flood control projects.
Bonz Dolor/Facebook
Former DPWH official Juliet Calvo, who faces charges over a P289.5-million dike project, will be returned to jail even after suffering a stroke

items: Juliet Calvo, a former public works official, will not be allowed to serve her detention at home despite suffering a stroke, as ruled by the Sandiganbayan.
Her lawyers requested home detention for better care and to alleviate financial strain from hospital bills, but the court decided that the jail could provide adequate medical support.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A former public works official facing a corruption case together with fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co will not be allowed to serve her detention at home, despite suffering a stroke, the anti-graft Sandiganbayan has ruled.

Juliet Calvo, once head of the maintenance division of the Department of Public Works and Highways in the Calabarzon region, remains in custody as a defendant in the case against Co, former representative of the Ako Bicol party-list, over alleged irregularities in a P289.5-million infrastructure project in Oriental Mindoro.

The Sandiganbayan’s 6th Division, in a September 10 decision, rejected Calvo’s request for house arrest. Instead, it gave her 30 days of continued confinement at the Philippine Heart Center from September 11, while she recovers from the stroke. She is due to return to the Quezon City Jail-Female Dormitory on October 11.

blocks.caption: LIST: DPWH officials arrested over flood control project in Oriental Mindoro

blocks.text: Calvo is charged with the resigned congressman with malversation of public funds in connection with the construction of a road dike along the Mag-Asawang Tubig River in Tagumpay, Naujan, Oriental Mindoro.

In a letter to the court, Jail Chief Inspector Aubrey Gutierrez said Calvo was taken to the Quezon Memorial Medical Center on August 5 after suffering a stroke. When she regained consciousness, she supposedly had difficulty communicating and was unable to move parts of her body.

She was later transferred to The Medical City on Ortigas Avenue in Pasig City because the first hospital lacked the equipment needed to treat her condition. From there, she was brought to the Philippine Heart Center in Quezon City, where she remained confined.

At a September 2 hearing, Calvo’s physician, Anthony Lontoc, said there was no assurance that she would recover the ability to walk or speak normally. He also said it was unclear whether she would eventually be able to eat or manage her personal needs without assistance.
Her lawyers sought permission for Calvo to continue her detention at home after leaving the hospital, saying she could receive care there from relatives and private medical professionals.
They also pointed to the growing hospital bills, which they said were placing an increasing strain on her family.
Prosecutors agreed that Calvo should remain hospitalized for the time being but objected to transferring her custody to her home.

Jail Chief Inspector Aubrey Gutierrez, meanwhile, told the court that the Quezon City Jail-Female Dormitory had two beds for patients, nurses available around the clock and two doctors who could be called when needed. While the jail clinic was not equipped to treat someone recovering from a stroke, she said its medical staff could provide nursing care and give Calvo the medicines prescribed by her doctors.
Gutierrez also cited a previous case in which the jail had cared for a bedridden person deprived of liberty who had suffered a stroke.
The court relied on the jail’s stated capacity to provide care when it turned down Calvo’s request to recover at home following her release from the hospital. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Datacentre company Firmus’s high flying valuation may be coming back down to earth ahead of expected ASX debut
articles.summary:
Sources say Firmus is slashing its price and may even shelve initial public offering altogether

The momentum behind Firmus Technologies’

blocks.text: The momentum behind Firmus Technologies’ high-flying valuation is showing severe cracks just weeks out from its anticipated ASX debut.

Multiple sources briefed on the matter told Guardian Australia the AI datacentre company is slashing its valuation to entice sceptical investors – or may even shelve its initial public offering altogether.

On Thursday, Firmus abruptly withdrew from its scheduled appearance at a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence amid harried discussions to save what was billed as the largest IPO in Australia in decades.
‘Fanciful’
Most of the alarm bells about Firmus have been centred on its near $44bn valuation for a company still in its start-up phase.

Its backers were confident of obtaining this valuation just days ago, but are now frantically re-pricing to find a level that investors will be comfortable paying ahead of an anticipated ASX listing late this month.
“The whole thing was getting fanciful,” said one investment manager briefed on the float.
“It’s a business that’s losing hundreds of millions of dollars, and yet its valuation kept going up nonstop every couple of months.”
In the lead-up to its anticipated listing, Firmus raised money from large investors, including chip maker Nvidia, and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue.
Just over a year ago, Firmus was worth less than $2bn, according to the value placed on it by Nvidia and others as they took equity stakes.
In just over a year, successive capital raising by many of the same core investors drove Firmus’s valuation from $1.85bn to $15bn about eight weeks ago.
That increased to almost $44bn just days ago, although that figure is being heavily unwound due to tepid support.
Key risk facing investors

Firmus has an enticing story to sell given it is designed to cash in on surging AI expenditure by building and operating liquid-cooled “AI factories” packed with Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), or chips.
But the key risk facing investors isn’t whether AI will keep growing, it’s whether they are paying too much for a company facing many operational obstacles.
Firmus only has two small operational sites alongside seven contracted and four planned facilities.
While it has contracts in place with Meta, OpenAI and Nvidia, about 97% of the contracted revenue sits on sites that aren’t yet built, according to Minotaur Capital co-founder Armina Rosenberg.
“You only get near the offer price if delivery, financing and renewals all go to plan,” said Rosenberg.

Its high valuation, and anticipated future earnings to support it, rely on the prompt construction of that unbuilt pipeline, at the exact moment that local communities are rebelling against similar developments.

While Firmus’s focus on Asia avoids the growing community backlash against datacentres in Australia – and the US – it comes with its own hurdles, such as power constraints and construction times, says Rosenberg.
Not empty hype
Firmus’s high valuation also assumed that the current, heavy AI expenditure from the so-called hyperscalers, like Microsoft, Google and Meta, continues, unabated.
When that expenditure slows, it will be the third-party datacentres that could be among the first to feel the cold.

Drawing on economist Charles P Kindleberger’s classic five-stage bubble framework - displacement, boom, euphoria, distress, and revulsion - Morningstar analyst Lochlan Halloway warned that market sentiment surrounding Firmus had entered the euphoric phase.
That doesn’t mean Firmus is empty hype, Halloway said, rather, the risk lies in whether investors are paying far too steep a price.
Firmus’s plans to list on the ASX on 23 October, in what would have been the largest IPO since Telstra in 1997, are now in doubt.
Investors were going to be asked to pay $11 per share. That price will either be radically reduced, thereby slashing its valuation, or the float will be withdrawn altogether.
Firmus was contacted for comment.

items: Jonathan Barrett is Guardian Australia’s business editor.

articles.title: Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
articles.summary: After Flavio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of Brazil's presidential election, thousands of people joined student-led protests against the far-right in Rio de Janeiro.

image.caption: Thousands of students took to the streets of Rio de Janeiro in protest against Flavio BolsonaroImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands of people joined a student march in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday to protest against the possibility of Flavio Bolsonaro becoming president after the far-right candidate came out on top in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, won around two million more votes than the incumbent president, the left-leaning Lula da Silva.
But since neither reached the 50% hurdle to win the presidency, the pair will face off in a run-off on October 25, in which Bolsonaro is considered the favorite.

blocks.caption: 'No to Flavio and yes to education,' read one signImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: "If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States," said 20-year-old literature student Joao Victor Vieira, voicing the fear of many on the left in Brazil that Bolsonaro is too ideologically aligned with US President Donald Trump.
Brazil: 'Never again Bolsonaro'

Other marchers held signs with messages such as "Brazil isn't anyone's backyard," "I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil," and "Never again Bolsonaro" – all against a soundtrack of drums, fireworks and chants.

blocks.caption: 'Brazil is not the backyard of the US,' read one protester's signImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We're fighting for Brazil, not for Lula," said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental sciences student, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, often worn by nationalist Bolsonaro supporters but which opponents have been aiming to reclaim for themselves.
"We don't have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people," she told the Associated Press.

blocks.caption: 'Fascists in jail, people in the streets,' this protester wrote on a Brazilian flagImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Alice Carneiro, a 25-year-old maritime shipping administrator, the prospect of another Bolsonaro conjures fears of far-right policies which will discriminate against Brazil's minorities – such as her transgender wife.
"I'm here because I believe in democracy," she told the AFP news agency. "Because I'm scared."
Witnesses reported that the march was notably more crowded and animated than President Lula's rally on the same street on Friday, the culmination of a lackluster campaign ahead of the election.
After the third, fourth and fifth places all went to right-wing candidates, who polled over eight million votes between them, Lula and the left appear to have a mountain to climb in the run-off.

The incumbent's campaign has shifted its focus to social media, where the far-right dominates but Lula has largely been absent, arguing he "like[s] to say only what is essential." But on Wednesday, the president convened leftist influencers who won legislative seats on Sunday to advise his campaign.

articles.title: Leviste intends to personally post bail amid arrest warrant, spox says
articles.summary: Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste intends to return to the Philippines and personally face the court to post bail amid an arrest warrant against him, his spokesperson said Thursday.

blocks.text: Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste intends to return to the Philippines and personally face the court to post bail amid an arrest warrant against him, his spokesperson said Thursday.
Interviewed on GMA News’ Unang Balita, Leviste’s spokesperson, Atty. Tony La Viña, was asked if the lawmaker will personally face the case and post bail.
“Oo. In general ang sagot ko, sa kaso kasi medyo subjudice na kasi ‘yan. Pero ang masasabi ko lang ay actually napakaliit ng kaso na ito. Tulad ng sinabi niya, this is a very small case,” he said.
(Yes. My answer to the case is in general because it is somewhat subjudice. But all I can say is that this case is actually very small. As he said, this is a very small case.)

“Almost insignificant. Bailable by 72,000 bail, very small penalty at lahat. So, in the scheme of things hindi naman ito ganun ka-importante from his point of view. Kaya naglabas nga siya ng statement na not to worry about him hindi naman siya abala dito hindi siya worried about this case,” he added.

(Almost insignificant. Bailable by 72,000 bail, very small penalty and all, so in the scheme of things, it’s not that important from his point of view. That’s why he released a statement saying not to worry about him, he’s not worried about this case.)
Leviste is in France with his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, who has been on medical leave since August 3.
Return
According to La Viña, Leviste has plans to return to the Philippines.
“Of course. I mean, eventually, uuwi naman yan siya kasama ng nanay niya,” he said.
(Of course. I mean, eventually, he will go home with his mother.)
“Right now lang talaga, kailangan siya ng nanay niya for the medical treatment of her mother. So, as far as I know, once tapos na yun. Uwi na siya. He is the only family of the mother,” he added.
(Right now, his mother really needs him for her medical treatment. So, as far as I know, once that's done, he will go home. He is the only family of his mother.)
La Viña also said Leviste would challenge any attempt to cancel his passport.
Asked about the possibility of an INTERPOL red notice, he said he did not expect it to apply to Leviste's case.
“From what I know, hindi siya applicable kasi (it is not applicable because) that applies only to very serious crimes,” La Viña said.
La Viña maintained that the case against Leviste was part of what he described as harassment or persecution against the lawmaker.
He linked the cases to Leviste's campaign against alleged corruption in flood-control projects.
The lawyer also defended Leviste's renewable-energy businesses, saying there was no wrongdoing in his solar franchise and service contracts.

He said the solar franchise was not implemented because the Department of Energy (DOE) had yet to issue the necessary implementing rules and regulations (IRR) and identify the locations where it could operate.
As for Leviste's service contracts, La Viña said some had been implemented while others had not, which he described as normal in the renewable-energy business.
La Viña said he had no information on whether Leviste would return to the Philippines ahead of or together with Legarda.
A Makati court has issued an arrest warrant against Leviste over an alleged violation of the Public Service Act.
Bail was set at P72,000.
EXPLAINER: What is the Public Service Act?

The DOE in May filed a complaint with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against Leviste and five officials of the Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation (SPBC) for alleged violations of the Public Service Act.

According to the complaint, the firm failed to construct and provide electric power to customers and end users in remote, unviable, unserved, or underserved areas as provided under the company’s 2019 franchise, which Congress granted under Republic Act No. 11357.
The complaint identified Leviste as the firm's chairman, president, chief executive officer, and director.
Leviste has denied the allegations. —Joviland Rita/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
articles.summary:
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom

Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon…

blocks.text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.

She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.

“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.
Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

articles.title: Winnipeg sex offender who flew under family's radar by changing name gets 15 years for abusing child
articles.summary: A convicted sex offender who sexually abused a 13-year-old boy whose family didn't know about the man's criminal past because he'd changed his name has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.

image.caption: Ryan James Knight, seen here in a 2024 photo, was sentenced in Winnipeg on Wednesday. He was convicted earlier this year of sexual interference and making child sexual abuse and exploitation material. (Submitted by Danielle Gzebb)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
A convicted sex offender who sexually abused a 13-year-old boy whose family didn't know about the man's criminal past because he'd changed his name has been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Ryan Knight 'leaving a trail of trauma' behind him, judge says
WARNING: This article contains details of child sexual abuse.
Ryan James Knight pleaded guilty in July to sexual interference and making child sexual abuse and exploitation material from August 2024 to March 2025.

Court heard Wednesday the boy's family had hired Knight, who was in his early 40s at the time, to renovate their basement. Knight then ended up hiring the child to do odd jobs around his own home down the street, where the repeated abuse happened.

Several years before, Knight had changed his last name from Gabourie. That meant that when the boy's family tried to look into Knight, they didn't find that he'd been convicted roughly two decades earlier of breaking into children's homes and sexually assaulting them as their families slept.
"They were duped," provincial court Judge Kael McKenzie said as he handed down Knight's sentence, after a joint recommendation from lawyers.
"It's not just one person that you hurt. It's over and over and over again, and for a long time…. You're just leaving a trail of trauma behind you, and for decades now."

The abuse came to light after Knight was out driving in a truck with the boy after midnight in March 2025, and ended up being pulled over by police. When officers found Knight had no familial relationship with the boy, they started an investigation that eventually uncovered Knight had been repeatedly sexually abusing the child.
Undated pictures of Knight released by Manitoba Justice in January 2024. (Manitoba Justice)

The boy, who can't be identified because of a publication ban, told police Knight would take him to the movies and let him sleep over at his house, and that he occasionally lent the boy a cellphone and let him play on his computer, an agreed statement of facts read by Crown attorney Katie Dojack said.

Investigators later seized electronics from Knight, which revealed child sexual abuse images of the boy. That led to police notifying the boy's parents that he'd been sexually assaulted and requesting to speak with him. The boy agreed but asked that his parents not be provided his video statement to watch.

The boy told police he didn't initially disclose anything to Child and Family Services when they became involved because he didn't trust them and "worried they would tell his dad," the agreed facts said.

items: Man charged with sexual assault of 2 teen boys after families built 'trusting relationship' with him: police

blocks.text: "He told police that he was embarrassed to talk about the accused and that the accused had warned him not to tell anyone."
During the investigation, the boy also told police Knight used to have another boy "hanging out with him." That child was later confirmed to be 14.

That boy's mother told police she'd known Knight for nine years, and her son occasionally slept over at his home. However, she cut off contact when her family members raised concerns and she noticed the boy was "behaving differently."
While police initially said Knight was charged with sexually abusing two teens, court records show other charges against him were stayed.
Light in boy's eyes 'replaced by anger'
The father of the boy whose son Knight was convicted of abusing said the boy, "who once openly showed his love for his family, has changed."
"Since what happened to him, he has often expressed anger toward us, and the light in his eyes seems to have been replaced by anger," the father wrote in a victim impact statement Dojack read.
"We hope that he will regain that spark, but we do not know whether he will."
He said while he searched Knight's name online before hiring him, he only found one complaint about a job he'd done.
"I believe his change of last name prevented me from discovering that history," the father said.

items: Brandon man sentenced to 25 years for sexual abuse of foster children

blocks.text: The boy's grandmother said she watched her grandson change from "a happy-go-lucky child into a very angry and sullen child."

"I watched the sparkly twinkle in his eyes disappear," she wrote in her victim impact statement. "He didn't believe we could help him, because Ryan had convinced him that his family didn't care about him and wouldn't believe him."
Prosecutor Dojack said sexual victimization can be especially shameful for boys "because of social expectations that males are supposed to appear tough."
"Embarrassment, humiliation and homophobia form a particularly toxic and stigmatizing combination for male child victims," she said. "I think that is certainly something to be considered here."
Knight's lawyer, Theodore Mariash, told court his client's childhood was also marked by "horrific abuse."
When given the chance to speak for himself, Knight apologized for the harm he caused to people sitting in the courtroom gallery and for taking away their right to know about his past.

items: 'No shame in being a victim': lawyer, social worker confront childhood abuser in court during sentencing
Man sentenced to 25 years for 'horrendous' sexual abuse after survivors spoke out

blocks.text: "I can't even imagine what it's like to learn who you had sitting at your dinner table," he said from the prisoner's box. "And I'm really sorry for that. No one deserved anything I have done."

Court heard Knight has a little over 13 years left on his sentence, with enhanced credit for time served. He's also subject to a list of conditions, including not contacting either of the children mentioned in the agreed facts.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: Suspect behind South Korea bank hacks may be 26-year-old in China
articles.summary: CrowdStrike says the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration-testing tool, alongside large language models

blocks.text: HACKER. A man holds a laptop computer as cyber code is projected on him in this illustration picture taken on May 13, 2017.
REUTERS/Kacper Pempel/Illustration/File Photo
CrowdStrike says the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration-testing tool, alongside large language models
SEOUL, South Korea – The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea’s financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China’s Guangdong province, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said.

In a report published on its website on Wednesday, October 7, CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analyzing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October.

CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models, and assessed with “moderate confidence” that the actor was a Chinese speaker and likely financially motivated.
The firm said one Claude Code session contained a request to create a security researcher resume describing results from the hacking activity.
The prompt included details such as a Telegram account, age, education background and a location in Maoming, Guangdong, the report said.

CrowdStrike said the same Telegram username appeared in other cyber activity, including vulnerability research involving a Telegram-based NFT marketplace and a separate suspected attack on a Chinese payment platform.
The company said the personal details likely belonged to the actor responsible for the activity, but cautioned that currently available information could not definitively identify the attacker.
Authorities in Seoul are investigating cyberattacks that affected multiple financial institutions after banks including Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank reported data breaches.
South Korean police, who have launched a probe, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday, October 6, that signs had emerged that AI was used in some of the hacking incidents and called for heightened cybersecurity measures. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump, who waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on Wednesday, October 7, that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize but acknowledged doubt about his chances.

“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said of the 2026 award, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Friday. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has repeatedly said he deserves what may be the world’s most prestigious award.

“It is about that time,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “But I was very honored to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.”
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her 2025 Nobel Peace Prize medal to Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts in Venezuela.

blocks.caption: 287 nominated for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, Trump likely among them

blocks.text: Trump said he should get the prize after wading into eight conflicts since taking office last January.
The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.

Parties to some conflicts Trump claims to have resolved dispute the US president’s diplomatic role, and fighting has flared again in some of those regions, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and along the border between Cambodia and Thailand.

A resolution to Russia’s war in Ukraine has eluded Trump, who promised to end it on the first day of his second White House term. US-Israel strikes on Iran have led to a seven-month simmering conflict that has upended global energy supplies and driven gas prices up before November’s midterm elections.
Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court, the special rapporteur for the Palestinian Territories, are among the favorites to win this year. – Rappler.com
