articles.title: U.S. army moves to execute man convicted in 2009 deadly Fort Hood rampage by firing squad
articles.summary: The former U.S. army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first U.S.…

image.caption: U.S. Maj. Nidal Hasan, the army psychiatrist who was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting rampage, is seen in a booking photo in April 2010. The U.S. army is moving to execute Hasan by firing squad in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The former U.S. army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first U.S. military execution in more than 65 years.
Few details have been released about who would be part of the firing squad or what procedure they would use

Acting secretary of the U.S. army Adam Telle said in a social media post that army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. This followed news from the Pentagon that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved the execution.

The announcement stunned an attorney who had represented Hasan in a civil case, and raised concerns among experts on military law about whether the army followed its mandated process for setting an execution and notifying a prisoner they've been condemned to death.

It also sparked questions about how a firing squad would be assembled and what procedure it would use. The last time the military executed someone by firing squad was shortly after the Second World War.
Here's a look at the military execution process and how experts say this case may proceed.

A man and child lay flowers and a balloon outside the front gate of the Fort Hood Army Post in Fort Hood, Texas following the shooting rampage which left 13 people dead in 2009. (Jessica Rinaldi/Reuters)
Who would form firing squad

Telle confirmed in his post on X that Trump had approved the execution on Oct. 2, starting the clock in army regulations that requires an execution date to be set no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after that approval.

Telle also noted that the execution would be carried out by firing squad, but did not offer details of where on base the execution would take place, what personnel would be a part of that squad or what procedure they would follow.

The Associated Press asked both Pentagon officials and the army for more details, but those requests were declined. A message to the army seeking comment on the potential procedural issues was sent Wednesday.

The procedures for execution in army regulations do not contain specific protocols for particular methods of execution. Experts said in previous iterations of the firing squad — nearly 80 years ago — one shooter would be given a blank so they all could plausibly believe they had not fired the fatal shot.
The execution could be delayed

Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims — a defence a military judge barred him from presenting during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

"What happens now, is if Dr. Hasan decides he wants to resist execution, he can go to federal civilian court for a Habeas Corpus petition … and that can last years," said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Habeas Corpus is a legal procedure whereby an incarcerated person can challenge the lawfulness of their imprisonment.
"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," Fidell said.

items: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan sentenced to death
Hasan guilty in Fort Hood U.S. army massacre

blocks.text: Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Military executions rare

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and the last execution that took place there was a hanging in 1961.

John Galligan, a retired colonel and a former military judge, represented Hasan in civil matters. The attorney said Wednesday that he's limited on what he can talk about, but called the rush to conduct the execution "horrific."

items: Fort Hood massacre trial a rare U.S. military execution case

blocks.text: Galligan, who spoke with Hasan on Wednesday, said he believes the army regulation to have the facility's army commandant notify Hasan, accompanied by a chaplain and a Trial Defence Service attorney or civilian counsel if possible, was not followed. Galligan said that, according to Hasan, there was no legal counsel present.

"For the life of me, I don't know what they are trying to accomplish in such a rush fashion … and by trying to conduct this execution at Fort Hood, when he has such medical issues," Galligan said, raising questions about how Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair, would be transported to Fort Hood.
How South Carolina conducts firing squads

Before Hasan's execution was set for Fort Hood, there was speculation the army might reach out to one of the handful of states that have recently reinstated the firing squad for use in executions — particularly South Carolina or Utah, where they've renovated facilities and established protocols.
South Carolina has killed three prisoners by firing squad in the past 18 months, the only such executions in the U.S. in the past 16 years.

It's unclear if the army will borrow from the state's protocol, but it sets out for three volunteer shooters to stand 4.6 metres from the condemned prisoner, who is strapped to a chair. A medical professional uses an X-ray to find the prisoner's heart and place a target over it. A hood is placed over the prisoner's head after his final words, and a shade is lifted so the shooters can see their target.
All three shooters have live ammunition and fire at the same time with no verbal warning for the condemned prisoner.
South Carolina spent about $54,000 US to renovate its death chamber for the firing squad.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Palace: DOH ‘closely monitoring’ plague concerns in Russia
articles.summary: The plague concerns came following the death of a laboratory technician in Russia who was working at a plague research institute.

blocks.text: This photo shows a woman walking past the logo of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's consumer and health watchdog in Moscow on October 5, 2026.
AFP / Igor Ivanko

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang assured the public on Wednesday, October 7, that the Department of Health (DOH) has started to monitor the plague risk in Russia, although international health officials said there were no signs of an outbreak.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing in Singapore that the state’s health department is following the recommendations of the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding concerns about the plague.

“Rest assured po sa mga kababayan natin po na nakatutok po ang DOH at kung ano man po ang kinakailangan pang gawin, ‘yun po ay kanilang gagawin. So far ay nami-meet naman po nila ang mga requirements para maibsan ang takot natin tungkol dito sa plague na nangyayari sa Russia,” Castro said.

(Rest assured, our fellow countrymen, that the DOH is focused on the concerns, and whatever needs to be done, they will do that. So far, they are meeting the requirements to relieve our fears about the reported plague in Russia.)
The plague concerns came following the death of a laboratory technician in Russia who was working at a plague research institute.
Authorities are investigating whether the lab technician died of pneumonic plague, raising global concerns.
The WHO, however, stressed that there is no need to be alarmed as no signs of a wider outbreak were detected.
Plague refers to an infectious disease primarily affecting rodents and micromammals and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which is the most dangerous form of plague, infects the lungs and can be transmitted from person to person through droplets released from breathing, coughing, or sneezing.

articles.title: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time
articles.summary:
The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants

Patricia Krenwinkel, a former Charles Manson follower, was granted parole…

blocks.text: Patricia Krenwinkel, a former Charles Manson follower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.

This is the third time that Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions and denied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.

Krenwinkel, who was 21 at the time of the 1969 killings, has been imprisoned longer than any other woman in California, and the parole board has repeatedly acknowledged her record of rehabilitation over 57 years in prison, concluding she would not in her elderly age be a danger to society.

She was convicted in 1971 for her role in the violent crime spree over two nights that claimed the lives of actor Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her four friends, and grocery owner Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. The killings were gruesome and became one of the most notorious crime stories in the US.
Krenwinkel was 19 years old when she “fell under Charles Manson’s control” and was exploited and psychologically abused by the cult leader, her attorneys have said.

“Reaching this moment has taken decades of hard, deliberate work to confront who she was, what she did, and the devastating harm she caused,” her longtime lawyer, Keith Wattley, said in a statement after the parole grant. “She fully accepts responsibility for her actions, everything she contributed to, and every life she destroyed in 1969. Pat does not excuse or minimize that harm.”

Over her decades in prison, Krenwinkel has had a clean disciplinary record, and nine consecutive psychological evaluations in the past 40 years have found her to be a low public safety risk, according to Wattley, who has represented Krenwinkel for 16 years. He said she has participated in extensive therapy and group counseling, earned a college degree and trained service dogs for people with disabilities.
“I have seen the depth of her remorse and the extraordinary work she has done to change her life. I firmly believe she is ready to return home,” Wattley added.
Debra Tate, Sharon Tate’s sister, has repeatedly objected to the release of Krenwinkel and other Manson followers.

When Newsom denied Krenwinkel parole in 2022, after the board first found her suitable for release, the governor acknowledged that she had been a “victim of Mr Manson’s abuse” and said she had “matured in prison and engaged in commendable rehabilitative efforts”. But he argued she had “not developed sufficient insight into the causative factors of her crime and her triggers for antisocial thinking” and was still dangerous.

When Newsom again denied her parole in 2025, he also acknowledged her “serious chronic medical conditions” had diminished her strength, but concluded she “must do additional work to deepen her insight before she can be safely released”.
The governor is required to consider her elderly age and that she committed the crime as a youth in his review of her case.

Krenwinkel’s attorneys and advocates have repeatedly argued the governor was caving to political pressures by denying parole to people convicted in high-profile cases. Newsom previously vetoed the release of Leslie van Houten, another former Manson follower, but an appeals court sided with her and granted her freedom in 2023. Newsom also faced scrutiny for overturning the parole grant of Sirhan Sirhan, convicted of assassinating Robert F Kennedy, even after two of Kennedy’s sons favored his release.

The push for Krenwinkel’s release comes at a time of growing concern about the increasing number of elderly people languishing in US prisons after decades of incarceration. Krenwinkel’s longtime friends from inside California’s women’s prison told the Guardian last year that she was a mentor and support system to others in the prison.

Wattley, founder of UnCommon Law, a non-profit organization that represents people at parole hearings, urged Newsom to “uphold the law” and approve Krenwinkel’s freedom: “The parole process exists because people can change, rehabilitation matters, and public safety must be grounded in evidence. Pat’s case raises a fundamental question: if three parole grants don’t lead to release, what is the point of this process?”
Spokespeople for Newsom did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Wednesday.

articles.title: Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year
articles.summary:
Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds

The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of…

blocks.text: The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.
The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.
The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.

The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds. Many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, with the bendy tree now the last one standing.

blocks.caption: Newcastle’s bendy elm. Photograph:  Michael Cooper

blocks.text: “When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.
“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.
For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.
Having grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.

“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”
The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.
“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey. Photograph: Lee Cooper

blocks.text: Other trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England. Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree. The roof of this room collapsed during a storm in 1845, but the tree lived on, with the wooden door to the secret room remaining to this day.
Also in the top 10 shortlist was the Culmstock Yew in Culmstock, Devon, England. This tree is perched on top a 20-metre high church tower, with its existence pre-dating residents’ living memories.

blocks.caption: Culmstock Yew in Devon. Photograph: Lee Cooper

blocks.text: Last year’s honour went to a 75ft ash tree that shades homes on one of Glasgow’s busiest roads.

The Woodland Trust has this week launched its Igniting Innovation competition for anyone aged 16 to 25 to share their ideas for projects that could benefit nature and make life better for woods, trees and people.
Three winners will receive £5,000 in funding and up to a year of expert mentoring to bring their projects to life.

articles.title: Average asking rent down 2.9% in B.C. in September, marking 2 years of decreases: report
articles.summary: A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation said the figures mark two full years of annual declines, the longest downturn the Canadian rental market has experienced in recent history.

image.caption: A report has found that average asking rents across Canada have been dropping for 2 straight years. (David Horemans/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation said the figures mark two full years of annual declines, the longest downturn the Canadian rental market has experienced in recent history.
Average asking prices in September across Canada were down 7.3% over the last 2 years
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 07, 2026 6:50 PM EDT | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
The average asking price for a rental unit in Canada in September was $2,034, down 4.2 per cent compared with a year ago.
Average asking rent prices in September were down 7.3 per cent over the past two years, and 9.2 per cent below the peak of $2,202 in May 2024.

The report also highlighted figures from Statistics Canada that show average weekly earnings have risen 19.4 per cent over the past five years, signifying a general improvement in rental affordability.
More GTA tenants are falling behind on rent. Here's why
Rents edged slightly lower on a monthly basis, down by $1 compared with $2,035 in August, a second consecutive monthly decrease.
The report said this is part of a typical seasonal pattern where demand rises in the spring and summer and begins to ease in the fall.
Across the provinces, average rents for all property segments were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year in Ontario, 2.9 per cent in B.C., 2.6 per cent in Alberta and 1.7 per cent in Quebec.

items: Asking rents drop again, but B.C. remains among Canada's most expensive markets
Backlash over rental prices at Sen̓áḵw development in Vancouver

blocks.text: In contrast, other provinces saw increases, including 1.4 per cent rises in both Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan.
On a per-square-foot basis, average asking rents in Canada's six largest markets came in at $2.48, falling 1.5 per cent from September 2025.
Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.7 per cent on an annual basis to an average of $2,036 in September, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 7.8 per cent to $2,052.
Rental prices for purpose-built apartments saw the smallest annual decline across all property types.
Condo rents saw the steepest declines, led by a 9.6 per cent drop in studio condo rents. Other secondary market units like houses and townhomes fell 7.4 per cent year-over-year to $2,016.
The report said rental markets in Toronto and Vancouver are showing signs of stability though after rents hit their lowest level in five years.
Average asking rent in Vancouver dips in the past year, report finds

"Our research shows supply has been the main driver of this correction, and in key markets like Toronto and Vancouver, new supply is moving past its peak," Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand said in a statement.

"Rents in both cities have trended higher over the past six months, and annual declines have narrowed significantly as renters come off the sidelines. Where Toronto and Vancouver go, the rest of the country follows."
A few factors support an "upcoming return to positive rent growth" in those cities, the report said.

This includes the fact that construction inventory has peaked, data revisions show a modest increase in populations, and both cities are relatively less exposed to tariffs across their respective labour markets.

"In the near term, more affordable rents and move-in incentives are releasing pent-up demand from delayed household formation, as higher rents in previous years led to prospective renters living with parents or roommates for longer," the report said.

articles.title: Lawyer accused of fraud says bad cheque didn't hurt the bank
articles.summary: The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.

image.caption: Suspended lawyer Nicholas Julian Cartel, accused of fraud for writing a bad cheque to allegedly cover a shortfall in his law firm's trust account, leaves a downtown Toronto courthouse on Monday during a break in his criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

blocks.text: The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth Tuesday on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.

Nicholas Cartel, a class-action and litigation specialist, is on trial on a single count of fraud over $5,000 relating to a $300,000 personal cheque he wrote in 2023, which prosecutors allege was done to help cover up the financial collapse of his and his wife’s law firm. That cheque bounced five days after being deposited into a TD bank account belonging to the law firm.

In the second day of testimony in provincial court in Toronto, a witness representing TD was grilled by both the defence and prosecution about what harm, if any, the bank incurred as a result. Proving fraud under the Criminal Code requires proving that someone either suffered a loss or was exposed to a risk of economic deprivation.
“There was no negative balance at the end of the day?” Cartel asked TD employee Tonya Cole in cross-examination.
“That’s correct, yes,” Cole replied.
Prosecutors Megan Rauser, left, and Dihim Emami converse outside court at the end of the first day of Cartel's criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Cartel has not denied he wrote the bad cheque for $300,000 on a personal account at RBC — which he maintains was a joint account with his wife, Singa Bui. But he says his wife, not he, deposited the cheque to the TD trust account of their firm, Cartel & Bui LLP. And then she was the one, he says, who immediately after obtained a $2.2-million certified cheque from TD to send to a client of the firm.

Prosecutors allege the certified cheque couldn’t have been issued without the top-up from the $300,000 deposit, because the law firm’s trust account was already in shortfall. Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
When Cartel’s personal cheque from RBC bounced five days later, TD had to go into his firm’s trust account and take out the $300,000.
Prosecutor Dihim Emami focused on that in his re-examination of Cole.

“It's fortuitous that this account had funds subsequent for TD to recover their $300,000, correct?” he asked. “If this account was depleted … or for a whole host of reasons other influxes of money didn't come in, TD might never have recovered that amount, correct?”
“That's possible, yes,” Cole said.
Home buyers and sellers left in lurch

The collapse of Cartel & Bui LLP in December 2023 left more than 25 home buyers and sellers in southern Ontario in the lurch for amounts ranging from $66,000 up to $2.16 million, in the case of one couple — money they had either transferred to the firm's trust account to buy a home or were expecting in payouts after selling their home.

Bui has admitted in lawsuits against her and Cartel that she started pilfering money from the firm’s trust account as far back as 2014 to fund the couple’s "luxury lifestyle," in a Ponzi-like scheme where incoming funds from new clients would cover for amounts she had stolen. She and Cartel bought two Toronto homes for $6 million total, sent their children to private school, took "luxurious vacations" and, she said, “decorated our home and office with elegant furnishings and expensive art.”

Cartel has long maintained he didn’t know about the embezzlement until December 2023, but a Superior Court judge overseeing more than 15 lawsuits against the couple and their former law firm has questioned those claims, saying at one point in June 2024: “Did she pay for nice gifts for you? Did you buy a car that she paid for? Did she pay mortgage payments? How can you not know, when you're living with her and you've got a home together and you've got children together, where $6 million went?"
The judge later sent both Cartel and Bui to jail, for 30 days and 20 days respectively, for contempt, ruling that they "have taken active steps to hide their finances and to frustrate the court."

Now-disbarred real estate lawyer Singa Bui leaves a Toronto courthouse in October 2024 after being sentenced to 30 days in provincial prison for civil contempt of court. The sentence was later reduced to 20 days. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

A Law Society of Ontario ruling in April 2024 suspending Cartel from practising law commented that “while it is conceivable that Ms. Bui acted alone and that Mr. Cartel had no knowledge or involvement, there are good reasons to believe otherwise,” including that various of Cartel’s explanations were “difficult to accept.”
Bui has since been disbarred while the Law Society’s disciplinary case against Cartel has yet to come to a final hearing.
Bogus signatures
In his criminal trial, Cartel is representing himself after a falling-out with his former defence lawyer Richard Posner.

Court records from a separate case, where Cartel challenged Posner’s invoices, show Posner criticizing Cartel for being “arrogant and patronizing” toward staff at Posner’s firm. Posner also told Cartel he was “completely uncomfortable” with Cartel’s wish to interact mainly over email “given the tenor of your writing.” Cartel had made claims in emails to Posner's firm that, among other things, the prosecution in his case had drafted a fraudulent document to pressure Cartel into agreeing to certain facts ahead of trial.

Cartel, in turn, accused Posner of “deliberate willful blindness” to documents that would supposedly help exonerate him. He also said Posner’s assistant “forced condescending, unsolicited opinions of culpability onto” him.

In another email, Posner states that if Cartel is going to testify in his own defence, it will take “a few days” to coach him because “without extensive preparation, Mr. Cartel will not present well as a witness.”

items: Lawyer couple accused of stealing millions from homebuyers while law society stalled
Lawyers at centre of $7M real estate embezzlement case charged with fraud

blocks.text: The dispute between them also reveals that Cartel put together documents that contained bogus signatures of another lawyer, George Tsimiklis. The signatures appear on the witness line of two affidavits Cartel swore in his dispute with Posner.

“Although the document bears my signature … I did not sign it either in person or electronically, and I did not authorize Mr. Cartel or any other person to affix or reproduce my signature on it,” Tsimiklis says in his own sworn statement filed in the case.
Cartel says the documents were only in draft form and he never intended them to be submitted to court.
Tsimiklis was a colleague of Cartel and has previously witnessed affidavits for him and represented Cartel’s wife, Bui.

Cartel told CBC during a break in his trial on Monday that he emailed the documents to a court clerk but only as drafts and he wasn’t formally filing them. He blamed the clerk for misunderstanding instructions and placing the affidavits with the bogus signatures into the court file.

items: Lawyer who admitted stealing millions of dollars from homeowners is disbarred

blocks.text: Asked how the signatures got onto his affidavits in the first place, Cartel claimed it happened because different pages from different documents got compiled together by the court clerk, including some pages that had Tsimiklis’s genuine signature from past filings.
That explanation, however, doesn’t square with the fact that Tsimiklis’s bogus signatures don’t appear on their own page but rather at the bottom of the newly created affidavits.
Cartel is currently suing CBC, Toronto Life magazine and the Toronto Sun newspaper for their coverage of his and his wife’s ordeals.
His trial is scheduled to resume in November.

articles.title: Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in new bill to fast-track development projects
articles.summary: A Liberal MP is calling for more guardrails as the Carney government moves to fast-track construction of projects like pipelines, mines and ports with a major piece of legislation currently before…

image.caption: Liberal MP Patrick Weiler, who represents a large riding in the Vancouver area, raised concerns over the sweeping powers planned in Bill C-39. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

A Liberal MP is calling for more guardrails as the Carney government moves to fast-track construction of projects like pipelines, mines and ports with a major piece of legislation currently before Parliament.
Patrick Weiler's comments are some of the first signs of Liberal dissent to Bill C-39
A Liberal MP is calling for more guardrails as the Carney government moves to fast-track construction of major projects like pipelines, mines and ports.
Liberal MP Patrick Weiler spoke in the House of Commons on Tuesday night, breaking ranks with his party on the Building Canada Strong Act, Bill C-39.
It's an early sign that concerns are starting to bubble up within the Liberal caucus about the Carney government's changes to Canada's environmental laws.
Weiler spoke about what he sees as C-39's shortcomings, but stopped short of explicitly calling for amendments to the bill.

items: Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment

blocks.text: Among the issues the MP flagged: too much discretion for ministers to exempt projects from environmental regulations, compressed timelines which may prevent Indigenous communities and NGOs from giving meaningful input and allowing construction to begin before an environmental assessment is complete.

Weiler is the MP for West Vancouver-Sunshine Coast-Sea to Sky Country. It's a massive federal riding where environmental concerns, particular over the construction of another pipeline to the Pacific coast, tend to resonate.
Weiler walking a tightrope
Seemingly walking a political tightrope in the House, Weiler aired his criticisms while still managing to support the intention behind the bill.

"We need the infrastructure that will connect Canadian products to new markets and make our economy more resilient," he said. "However, there is an important question we need to ask: Can we build faster without lowering the bar?"
Weiler said the answer is yes — adding he supports the overall "direction of this legislation" but called for more precautions to be built in.
He raised the issue that a future non-Liberal government could abuse the new powers the bill gives ministers and cabinet.

"Given that the powers in this bill would be permanent, it is important that where new flexibility or discretion is created, Parliament instils clear and transparent processes," Weiler said in his remarks.
The Carney government describes C-39 as one of the most important economic pieces of legislation in a generation, empowering regulators and ministers to greenlight projects within one year.
Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk
The legislation also includes changes to Canada's Labour Code, angering unions.
The bill allows ministers to make "technical, economic and practical" considerations when permitting construction in sensitive areas.
Weiler raised the concern that new economic lens for decision-making could lead the government to abandon environmental protections because they are too costly.
He said the cost of implementing a new plan to protect caribou, for example, should not be a factor when deciding whether a species or its habitat should be safeguarded.
"[Economic feasibility] should not become a substitute for achieving the environmental outcome," Weiler said.

Weiler seemed to be worried that the changes the government is proposing means communities would have less time to digest all the impacts and respond during environmental assessments — which typically offer the opportunity for those who live closest to have their say.
"Large proponents can have teams of consultants, scientists, engineers and lawyers, while smaller communities, local organizations and First Nations may not have that same capacity," Weiler said.
Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill
He suggested the government could solve this by boosting "participant funding, access to technical expertise, clear and accessible information."
"If we want a more efficient process, we also need to make sure that people have a fair opportunity to participate in it," Weiler said.

The legislation also allows shovels to hit the ground before the federal government gives a project the green light. This early construction is limited to unspecified preliminary activities that the environment minister considers are in the "public interest."
For Weiler, that wording is too vague.

"Parliament should be clear on what work can and cannot be done," Weiler said. "It should not be irreversible, it should not prejudge the final decision or replace the assessment itself and it should continue to respect Indigenous consultation and environmental requirements."
Weiler spoke in support of the bill's requirement for regional assessments — a study of the impact of development over a large area.

A regional assessment has been completed for wind development offshore of Nova Scotia. The 300,000-square-kilometre study area could unlock significant sustainable power generation for the province and the country.
"This gives us a chance to think about development at the scale of the ecosystem, rather than looking at small projects in isolation," he said.
Although C-39 touches on labour, nature and major projects, Transport Minister and House leader Steven MacKinnon is overseeing the bill's passage.
CBC News asked the minister's office if the Carney government was open to making changes to C-39 in line with concerns Weiler had raised, and did not immediately hear back.
Special committee for a special bill
C-39 is currently before the House of Commons. The Carney government plans to usea parliamentary tool not seen since the Harper government to prioritize study once it enters the committee phase.

The government is using a "legislative committee" to study the bill's more than 200 clauses. The mechanism was used for some of the most consequential laws in Canadian history, including the Clarity Act in 2000 and the 2005 Civil Marriage Act, which legalized same-sex marriage across the country.

items: Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era

blocks.text: A public letter from environmental groups called for the bill to be divided up and sent to relevant parliamentary committees with expertise on the more technical aspects of the bill such as the environment, fisheries and labour.

"Its many provisions require careful, expert scrutiny that cannot be adequately addressed through a single, newly formed committee alone," said the letter signed by a dozen environmental organizations.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: 'Unimaginable loss': Horses killed on B.C. highway while travelling to championship
articles.summary: Four horses were travelling from across Western Canada to compete in the Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship in Langley. Three were killed in a crash, and another was injured.

image.caption: Mackenzie Abbott is seen beside Fearless, a horse that was killed during a highway crash in B.C. while travelling to the National Dressage and Para Dressage Championships West in Langley on Oct. 6, 2026. (Submitted by Amelia Carter)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Four horses were travelling from across Western Canada to compete in the Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship in Langley. Three were killed in a crash, and another was injured.
Police say the driver hit a rock wall on Highway 1 in southeast B.C.; 3 horses killed and 1 injured in crash
The Canadian equestrian community is mourning the death of three horses after a collision in B.C.
The horses were travelling from Manitoba and Alberta to Langley on Monday, to compete in the 2026 Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship at the Thunderbird Show Park.
At 8:45 a.m. local time on Oct. 6, officers with the B.C. Highway Patrol responded to a single-vehicle crash roughly 40 kilometres east of Revelstoke on Highway 1.
The driver was towing a trailer with four horses when she lost control and collided with a rock wall, according to Sgt. Michael McLaughlin.
Three horses died, and the fourth horse was injured.
Kate Wall seen with Rosaria, a dressage horse that died during a single vehicle collision on Highway 1 in B.C. on Oct. 6, 2026. (Shealynn Choy/S.C.apturing The Moment Photography)
Paramedics with B.C. Emergency Health Services responded to the crash with an ambulance.
"Paramedics provided emergency medical care to one patient, who was transported to hospital in stable condition," said BCEHS paramedic public information officer Brian Twaites.
Police said the driver was a 73-year-old woman from Langdon, Alta.
"The driver was issued a violation ticket for failing to keep right under the [B.C.] Motor Vehicle Act, which comes with a fine of $109," McLaughlin said.
Condolences from all over Canada are pouring in for the horses and those who knew them.
'My heart is completely shattered'
Mackenzie Abbott is a dressage rider and head trainer from Headingley, Man. She said two of the horses were ones she trained, and they were owned by Solace Stables.
"We have suffered an unimaginable loss and lost our beloved horses," Abbott said. "I loved my horses more than I could ever explain. My heart is completely shattered."
The two horses, named Fearless and Rosaria, were set to compete in Langley starting on Oct. 9.

Highway 1 near the Illecillewaet Brake Check, roughly near where the collision occurred on Oct. 6, 2026, east of Canyon Hot Springs and Revelstoke. Four horses were in the trailer and three died. (DriveBC)
"They were the top of their fields in our sport here in Manitoba, and we were looking forward to proving their capabilities to Canada," Abbott said.
The two horses were being transported with a driver, and Abbott had flown to Abbotsford to meet them at the competition. When she landed, she received a phone call about the crash.
"We all fundraised to get there," Abbott said. "We are just devastated to lose our best friends in the most tragic way."
The competition was being organized by Equestrian Canada, and is a major national event where athletes and their horses travel to the West Coast to compete.
It is common in the sport for athletes and owners to hire commercial drivers to transport the horses to the events.

items: Olympic champion Eric Lamaze to step away from role with Equestrian Canada

blocks.text: In a statement, Equestrian Canada said it has reached out to the athletes and owners involved and extended mental health support.
"Our equestrian community functions as a close-knit family, and a sudden loss of this magnitude is felt deeply by every rider, coach, groom, and owner across the country," reads the statement
"[Equestrian Canada] extends its heartfelt sympathies to the riders, owners, families, and the entire support team surrounding these beloved horses."
James Hood, the chief of staff with Equestrian Canada, said they are organizing a fundraiser at the event to support the people impacted.
"I encourage our athletes, our coaches and our grooms and owners to lean on each other in this time of loss ... because it is a trying time and we will get through this," Hood said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Teen accused in school sword attack praised Nazis, talked about mass murder plans, court hears
articles.summary: In the months leading up to a sword attack at a Brandon high school, a teen allegedly wrote in a notebook about "invaders" of Canada — specifically African American and Muslim immigrants — and his…

image.caption: Police are seen on June 10, 2025, outside Neelin High School in Brandon, Man., where an attack with a sword led to the arrest of one teen and another being taken to hospital. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: This story contains references to violent crime and racially motivated attacks.

In the months leading up to a sword attack at a Brandon, Man., high school, a teen wrote in a notebook about "invaders" of Canada — specifically Black and Muslim immigrants — and his mass murder plan.

That's according to an agreed statement of facts presented in court Tuesday, as the trial for the boy began unexpectedly ahead of schedule in Brandon's Court of King's Bench. The day was originally scheduled for a pretrial hearing.

The now 17-year-old, who can't be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, pleaded not guilty to nine charges related to the June 10, 2025, attack at Neelin High School in the southwestern Manitoba city, including three charges of attempted murder.
He's also charged with aggravated assault, two counts of assault with a weapon, wearing a disguise with intent and two counts of possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.
As the charges were read out, the boy became emotional, prompting the judge to ask him if he needed a break.

The 2025 attack left a fellow 15-year-old student — who is Black and whose family is originally from Nigeria — with major injuries, in what police have previously described as a racially motivated crime.

items: Brandon teen recovering at home after sword attack inside high school

blocks.text: Details of the attack were revealed in court in an agreed statement of facts read by federal Crown prosecutor Hugh Crawley.
Just after 10 a.m. on the morning of the attack, the accused, then a Grade 10 student, told a friend on the phone that he was going through with the plan he'd been formulating for months.

Shortly after 1 p.m., he entered the school wearing black pants and a black trench coat, with a concealed sword and steak knife. He went to a washroom and put on a black "plague" face mask, which featured a long, beak-like nose and covered most of his face.
He then entered the east hallway of the high school, which has about 380 students in grades 9 to 12.
Brandon community cadets are seen outside Neelin High School in Brandon on Tuesday, June 10, 2025. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

The victim, a fellow student, stopped to tell the teen he liked the costume. They spoke for a few seconds before the accused stabbed the other teen multiple times in his shoulder, chest, stomach, thigh and arm.
The victim — a 15-year-old Grade 10 student — grabbed at the sword to try to prevent the attack, which severed one of his fingers and cut others.
That victim ran away, with the accused following, then ducked into the administration office.
He passed by the principal, Baseswa Nundu, who thought the victim was playing a joke. Soon after, the accused spotted the principal and chased him down the hall.
Nundu ran into a nearby classroom and held the door closed. The accused stabbed at a small glass window by the door, narrowly missing Nundu's eye.

The accused then walked down the hallway past several Caucasian students and didn't react, the agreed statement reads. He saw another student, identified in the statement only as B, and started chasing that student with his sword above his head.
A Caucasian teacher stopped the accused and was unharmed.
According to the agreed statement of facts read by Crawley, the accused entered a classroom and asked if there were "any blacks." The students told him no and the accused left.
'Why didn't you shoot me?'
By this point — about five minutes after the accused had entered the school — the principal had ordered a lockdown and the hallways were largely empty.
Seven minutes after the teen entered the school, Brandon police officers arrived. Nearly the entire Brandon police service was sent to the school, the statement of facts says.
The accused asked police to shoot him in the head and refused to drop the sword, the statement says.
Police used a Taser on him twice before he was taken into custody.
Once in custody, the teen shouted, "Why didn't you shoot me?" and "I wanted you to shoot me."
The teen "told every officer he encountered that he was intoxicated," according to the agreed statement of facts, but officers said he showed no signs of this.
More bloodshed intended in Brandon high school sword attack: police

In a videotaped interview with police, played in court Tuesday, the boy told detectives he'd been planning the incident for months and he'd gotten the sword from his home, saying it belonged to his sister. He said he practised with it in the bushes in his yard.
When pressed on his motive, he said he wanted to "go out with a bang" and hoped that would garner praise from certain people.
He admitted to being inspired by a 2015 case in Sweden where a man dressed in black and armed with a sword killed three immigrants before being killed by police.

items: Sword attack at Brandon high school was racially motivated act of hate, police say

blocks.text: In the interview, the teen told detectives he didn't attack Caucasian kids in the classroom because they were white.
He also used the term "invaders" to describe people he believed move to Canada but hate the country and do monstrous things to Canadians, the agreed statement of facts says.
"The accused told police the only thing that went different from his plan was that he was not killed by officers," the statement says.
Journal entries praised Nazis
A day after the attack, Brandon police combed through the accused's home.
In it, they found several cardboard weapons, in the shape of guns and swords, in the teen's room.
A black notebook with journal entries dating back to mid-2022 had several entries celebrating Hitler and the Nazis, and others supporting Texas's right to patrol its borders.

items: Manitoba Crown hopes to add terrorism provision to charges in 2025 sword attack

blocks.text: The notebooks also contained references to Black and Muslim immigrants, whom he called "invaders," the statement of facts says.
A Feb. 5, 2022, entry spoke of a hatred for Muslims, saying "with a gun, I'd spree kill as much … as I can."
A journal entry written 12 days before the Neelin school attack detailed a "mass murder" suicide plan.
Crown prosecutors say a phone seized during a search of the teen's home contained a file that they plan to argue was the beginning of a manifesto he wrote. (CBC)
Police also seized a tablet and phone belonging to the accused that had files about school shootings, including the 1999 shooting in Columbine high school in Colorado.

In the months leading up to the school attack, there were thousands of searches on the accused's phone for domestic terrorism, specific incidents of violence and targeted acts of racially motivated violence.
One search included average police response times in Brandon.

items: More stories from Southwest Manitoba

blocks.text: The phone contained 14,538 photos, including many of guns and other weapons, Hitler and other Nazi imagery, plus some pictures of himself giving a Nazi salute with cardboard weapons.
Several documents on his phone had titles referencing Hitler, white supremacy and school attacks. The phone also had several manifestos written by white nationalists.
Crown prosecutors also said the phone contained a file that they plan to argue was the beginning of a manifesto written by the accused.
Video footage from inside Neelin High School, which has over a dozen video cameras, according to the statement of facts, are expected to be shown in court during the trial.
The accused has been in custody since his arrest. His trial is scheduled to resume in June 2027.

articles.title: Isaias expected to become hurricane before hitting U.S. Gulf Coast, forecasters say
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters predicted it will quickly strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the…

image.caption: A satellite image from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows Tropical Storm Isaias off the eastern coast of Mexico on Wednesday. (U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters predicted it will quickly strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week.
Landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening

Communities in the potential path of Isaias moved quickly to prepare, with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production and an Alabama beach city cancelled a weekend festival known to draw thousands of tourists. Florida's governor declared a state of emergency for more than one-third of the state's counties.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday's college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, which U.S. President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
Isaias could become a major Category 3 hurricane, with winds of 178 km/h or stronger, before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center.
"We're expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend," Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday.
A late arrival

The storm was on track to tie or break a 121-year-old record as the latest arriving initial hurricane of the Atlantic season. According to the U.S. National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year's first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year due to a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average, where Tropical Storm Simon also formed Wednesday off Mexico.

The Miami-based hurricane centre on Wednesday issued a hurricane watch for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours.

items: Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo

blocks.text: Brennan says dangerous storm surge could affect an even wider area, from southeast Louisiana to Florida's Big Bend. Heavy rains of seven to 15 centimetres could trigger flash flooding near the coast, with accumulations of three to eight centimetres as far inland as Tennessee and the western Carolinas.

Isaias was centred about 365 kilometres northwest of Progreso, Mexico, and about 805 kilometres south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the hurricane center. It had maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h and was moving east-northeast at 13 km/h.

Forecasters predict Isaias will become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns north toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. Though its path and timing could shift, the storm is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.

Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that's no stranger to major hurricanes. One of the 20th century's worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Miss., in 1969.
Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighbourhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael levelled homes and buildings near Panama City, Fla., in 2018.
Gulf oil production, tourism already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

As of Wednesday, producers had temporarily halted about 25 per cent of the oil produced in the region, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect oil markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
"I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising," Burkhard said in an email.
In Gulf Shores, Ala., the storm threat caused organizers to cancel the National Shrimp Festival scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment.

In Pensacola, on the Panhandle, electric utilities were readying crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding.

articles.title: Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach
articles.summary:
In the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a…

blocks.text: The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.

In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called on Europe to “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.

The highly produced speech contained a forceful rejection of the kind of globalist politics that Trump has blamed for America’s and Europe’s ills, including growing illegal immigration and the outsourcing of manufacturing. In it, Rubio warned that the western world was at an “inflection point” and defended America’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.

“The word nationalism became a dirty word, so we tore down our monuments,” Rubio said. “We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the country they would inherit.”
Now, he said, the western world had found itself at a crossroads, where it either must “maintain its place at the head of the world or [resign] itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline”.

“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice,” Rubio continued. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”

The speech comes as relations between the US and Europe are facing numerous strains, including the US war in Iran, Washington’s scattershot support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia, disputes inside Nato including Trump’s recent demands for sovereignty over Greenland, and a growing ideological divide being driven by powerful officials including the US vice-president, JD Vance.

The shift in the Trump administration’s use of national power has unsettled many European allies, who have continued to seek compromises in order to keep the Trump administration onside on major issues including support for Ukraine and economic cooperation through the European Union.

Vance, a likely contender in the 2028 elections, put European allies on notice last year in a speech at the Munich security conference, when he accused leaders of being “terrified of their own people” and warned about the “threat from within” that Europe would reject values it shared with the US.
Rubio has developed a less aggressive – but nonetheless pointed – message of calling for European powers led by the US to fight against “civilisational erasure”.

Rubio addressed the tensions as he invoked Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address in 1861 on the eve of the civil war, saying: “Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.”

“Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age,” he said, extolling the recent agreement between the US, Denmark, and Greenland that he claimed will “reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of Nato.”

But the speech on Wednesday indicates that the shift in US geopolitical power may remain through a following presidency, as two of the most prominent Republican officials in the current administration have delivered forceful declarations to Europe that there will not be a return to the politics of the past.

On Wednesday, speaking to a crowd of 250 invited Greek and European officials, as well as journalists, Rubio sought to rally European allies, saying they should follow the example of the current government of Greece, to embrace a partnership with the US on everything from “everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally”.

“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said, pointing to positive tendencies including increases in European defense spending, expanded manufacturing and production, and a “flurry” of new partnerships and programs.

To bolster his case, Rubio delivered a selective reading of history from antiquity to the present, saying that the values of the Ancient Greeks imbued those of later scientists and explorers, including some controversial choices including Christopher Columbus and the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés, whose legacies are associated with the subjugation of Latin America.
But Rubio said they, as well as many others, carried a frontier spirit that was born in antiquity.

“The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world,” he said.

The Acropolis speech was heavily produced, with four cameras including one mounted on a crane, and was unusual for a secretary of state delivering a speech during a three-country swing through Iceland, Portugal and finally Greece.
In an unusual aside for the US’s top diplomat, Rubio also linked his own journey back to Europe, and then back to the Greeks of antiquity as well.

“Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the secretary of state of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish,” he said.

articles.title: Family of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’
articles.summary:
Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow

The family of a student who took his own life after being

blocks.text: The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.
Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.
However, his family said that in September that year, the university told him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.
His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.
He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.
Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.
The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.

blocks.caption: Tracy Scott, pictured after a meeting with the Scottish education secretary on Wednesday. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

blocks.text: On Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.
On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.
Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University of Glasgow on notice that they will be held to account”.
Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.
He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.

“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.
“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”

blocks.caption: The family’s solicitor, Aamer Anwar, claimed that the University of Glasgow had ‘forgotten its soul’. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

blocks.text: Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.

A spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.
“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.
“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.
“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”

A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.

articles.title: Why more than 250,000 people have joined student-led protests in France
articles.summary: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage.…

image.caption: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage. Students, pictured here in Bordeaux on Oct. 6, hold placards reading 'Surviving or studying' on the left

blocks.text: France has been thrown into crisis as student-led protests erupted across the nation, calling for better conditions for learning and for the government to address a decade-long staffing shortage.

Protests began at a Paris-region high school in mid-September, soon growing into a nationwide movement. More than 250,000 people took to the streets on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, the Interior Ministry said, in the demonstration's biggest day yet. (Organizers put the number higher, at 450,000.)

The rallies have led to widespread school disruptions, arrests and violence, with police deploying tear gas and other riot-control weapons against crowds of mainly teenagers — angering their parents and teachers and prompting them to participate.

It represents the latest test for outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. His prime minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday night, pledging to introduce new measures by the end of the month. A platform for students to voice grievances, launched on Tuesday, has already received some 40,000 submissions.
Here's a look at what we know so far about the protests — and how they became so widespread.
Protesters hold a banner reading 'Rostand angry, Rostand supportive' during the protest in Caen, France, on Oct. 6. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images)
Why are they protesting?

Many high school students say the state of their learning environment is poor, from decaying infrastructure to a lack of personnel. More than half of all schools are short-staffed this year, according to a survey conducted by a secondary school teachers’ union.

The shortage has affected public education in France for close to a decade. The chronic failure to replace absent teachers or hire substitutes means students can miss hundreds of hours of instruction.

items: India’s Cockroach Party shows frustrated Gen-Zers are hard to crush
Anti-government protesters clash with riot police in Mexico City during Gen Z-led rally

blocks.text: They are fed up with overcrowded classrooms, as well, which have increased to an average of 25 to 30 students a class.

Students also describe dilapidated buildings, pest infestations — including cockroaches and rats — and uninsulated classrooms severely affected by temperature shifts, particularly during recent heat waves.
“In the summer, it's 35 degrees,” said Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin. “And we're, like, 30 to 35 students in every class, so it's unbearable!”
Rudy Cuvilliez, who studies in the Paris suburb of Pantin, holds up canisters from tear gas he says police fired earlier in the day on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

Students and their supporters have taken to the streets for weeks because they feel the government is doing too little, too late. The Education Ministry will receive an additional €1.2 billion in funding next year, but it will not be enough, according to opposition parties, who say the amount barely keeps up with inflation.
Why is the state of schools so poor?
The French state spends more on education than on any other ministry, but it has not kept up with a sharp increase in the youth population, expected to peak in 2028.

The movement originated in the suburbs of the greater Paris region — areas historically underserved and facing significant growth. There are considerable regional disparities, with Île-de-France spending less than any other region in the country.
Schools in higher-income areas benefit from parents’ contributions, while those in underprivileged areas often lack resources.
Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting
Meanwhile, administrative and contracting procedures can be complex, meaning that even repairs that have been financed can take a long time to carry out.
As for personnel, teachers are not valued as they once were — entry-level salaries were more than double minimum wage in 1980; now, they are only just above the minimum.

“The government has not really made an effort to make the profession attractive," said Agnès Van Zanten, a senior research professor emeritus at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research, "such as by raising salaries, for instance.”

items: Gen Z toppled Bangladesh's autocratic regime. Will it decide the next government?

blocks.text: What do the students want?

Many want to see large-scale recruitment of teachers, school nurses and teaching assistants. Students, particularly in the banlieues, or economically deprived suburbs, call for urgent repairs and renovations to school buildings.
Recent educational reforms have resulted in longer school days, often extending from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., which many find onerous.

But students should be careful what they wish for: The French school day is so long in part to compensate for lengthy school vacations — some 16 weeks compared to the European average of 14. Shortening school days may mean fewer holidays.
A protester in Paris holds a sign that says, 'Is the revolution reserved for history classes?' in French on Oct. 6. (Kyle G. Brown/CBC)

What keeps other students awake at night is “Parcoursup,” a national web platform where high schoolers can secure a place in a higher education institution. Students can list up to 10 schools of preference, with their marks and test results included in their applications.
How they are assessed, however, is a bit of a mystery, with critics calling for the repeal or overhaul of the process.
It was among the topics raised by students meeting with the national education minister last week, but they reached no agreement, and school blockades resumed.
Wracked by weeks of student protests and an increasingly broad base of support, the French government is now trying to rush through a number of reforms.
What disruptions have the protests caused?

Since the movement began last month, hundreds of schools have been blockaded. And while the majority of protests have been peaceful, some have been marred by vandalism and violence. Police have made more than 5,000 arrests so far.
More than 200 people have been injured since the student mobilization began, “whether in accidents … or due to injuries caused by troublemakers,” said Education Minister Édouard Geffray.
Up to 500 schools in France to remain closed amid student protests

Police have also severely injured some people, including a youth who was blinded in one eye after being hit by a flash-ball. France has suspended the use of stun grenades after 15-year-old boy's hand was mutilated in northern France.

Amnesty International condemned “the disproportionate use of force against secondary school protests," calling for police to de-escalate. At least 18 internal police investigations are underway into alleged police violence.
Why has the response been so aggressive?

The Interior Ministry is applying a policy of “absolute firmness” to break up blockades and prevent the destruction of public property. Twenty-four schools had been burned or ransacked on Sunday, according to the education minister.

French police forces have often been criticized by human rights groups and the UN for their use of excessive force, and the response to the student protests has sparked intense controversy, not least among parents.
Teenager loses hand in violent France school protests

items: Police in France use tear gas, water cannons against student protesters
Macron government struggles to quell protests as riot police clash with high schoolers

blocks.text: Critics blame the prime minister and interior minister for inciting the police by insisting the movement was a problem of social order rather than trying to address students’ demands.
Why is the government worried about these protests?

Even though most of the protesters are under 18 — the minimum voting age in France — the government still sees the continued uprising as a threat to public order, particularly now that parents, teachers and activists of all kinds have joined in solidarity.

Indeed, the government is concerned about a potential “coalition of anger,” in which frustration with a decade under Macron reaches a boiling point. Historically in France, youth movements have often served as a catalyst for wider social movements and upheaval.

articles.title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution
articles.summary: Pike's lawyers have said she was very aware of Tennessee's failed execution effort. A judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence from the botched execution.

image.caption: Pike's lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute her sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her executionImage: George Walker IV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US judge told the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, whom lawyers say is "angry and confused" after waking up in hospital nearly a week after the ordeal.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for torturing and killing classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived despite being given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug.
What do we know about Christa Pike's current state?
One of her attorneys spoke about the 50-year-old's state after the failed execution.
"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Randy Spivey said during a news conference, adding Pike is "very aware" of what was done to her.

"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.
Pike is the only person known to have survived after receiving lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, said that "medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request."

Her lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike's sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her execution. The Republican governor had denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution.

blocks.caption: Demonstrations were held against Christa Pike's executionImage: George Walker IV/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pike's recovery period unclear
Experts say it is possible that the failed execution was due to a problem with the IV line that caused the injection to pool in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown," her attorneys wrote in their court filing.

Pike's arms were burned and blistered due to the injection, according to her legal team, who are demanding that the prison authority holds all information from the attempted execution, including needles and execution logs.
It is not yet clear how Pike's recovery might unfold and whether she will be subjected to another execution attempt.
