articles.title: Marcos to agencies: Prioritize food, fuel, electricity
articles.summary: President Marcos is zeroing in on efforts to ensure enough food, fuel and electricity supply after inflation soared to 7.2 percent last month due to the Middle East conflict and recent disasters,…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am

SINGAPORE – President Marcos is zeroing in on efforts to ensure enough food, fuel and electricity supply after inflation soared to 7.2 percent last month due to the Middle East conflict and recent disasters, Malacañang said.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said Marcos met with Executive Secretary Ralph Recto yesterday to discuss ways to ease the impact of rising prices.

“We are preparing for this. We cannot deny the effect of the ongoing crisis in the Middle East and the calamities that entered the Philippines. Even the political noise is affecting our economy,” Castro said.

“The President is now focusing on food, fuel and electricity. The directive of the President is to ensure that the Philippines will not run out of fuel supply. If the supply of fuel is disrupted, businesses would be disrupted and it would have a bigger effect on our economy,” she added.
Inflation quickened to 7.2 percent in September from 6.1 percent in August and 1.7 in the same month last year mainly due to higher food and energy prices.
Rice inflation accelerated due to tighter domestic supply and higher transportation costs.
Fish and vegetable inflation quickened due to weather disturbances that affected supply.
Castro gave assurance that the government will sustain policies and programs designed to assist vulnerable sectors.

She cited the removal of the 12-percent value added tax in the allowable system loss charge in electricity bills; the management of pork supply during the holiday season; the UPLIFT program, which involves interventions that aid sectors hit by the impact of the Middle East war; the TUPAD emergency employment program and free rice program. “The fuel subsidy for PUV (public utility vehicle) drivers will continue as well as the expansion of Kadiwa,” Castro said, referring to the program for accessible and affordable goods.
Castro said the government is also bracing for the effects of El Niño, which started this month and may last until March next year.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III and Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida will serve as caretakers while Marcos is out of the country.

articles.title: 80% of Pinoy children face violence – CEAP
articles.summary: Eighty percent of Filipino children have experienced some form of violence at home, school, workplace, community or in dating relationships, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
A child raises her hands to cover her face.
Pexels / Ksenia Chernaya

MANILA, Philippines — Eighty percent of Filipino children have experienced some form of violence at home, school, workplace, community or in dating relationships, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP) revealed as it called for stronger child protection measures in Catholic schools through a protocol.

“The CANE+D Protocol, covering Child Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation and Discrimination, should be a serious concern for Catholic education because the scale of violence against children in the Philippines tells us that child protection cannot remain at the level of policy statements,” CEAP said.

The association noted that aside from the 4th National Plan of Action for Children report, the United Nations Children’s Fund reported that three in five children experienced violent discipline, about one in three experienced school bullying and one in five children who use the internet have experienced sexual abuse or exploitation online.

In 2023 alone, the Philippine National Police Women and Children Protection Center received 18,756 reports of child rights violations, of which 17,304 involved violence against children, including child abuse, rape and acts of lasciviousness.

“These figures remind us that a school may be one of the places where a child first discloses harm or where warning signs are first seen. The revised CANE+D protocol therefore matters because it establishes a more coordinated pathway for identification, reporting, investigation, case management, legal proceedings, rehabilitation, reintegration and prevention,” CEAP added.
CEAP said the protocol brings teachers and other frontline workers into the protection system and calls for specialized training for personnel handling CANE+D cases.

The Department of the Interior and Local Government has directed local government units to adopt and implement the revised CANE+D Protocol and strengthen coordinated referral and case-management systems involving social workers, law enforcement, health professionals, educators and other frontline actors, CEAP said.

“For Catholic schools, this is ultimately a question of mission: when the dignity of a child is wounded, how prepared are we to recognize it, respond to it, protect the child and walk with the child toward healing?” it asked.

“Healing, therefore, cannot mean simply helping a child feel better after something has happened. In Catholic education, healing must include protection, truth, accountability, accompaniment, restoration, and the rebuilding of trust,” CEAP said.

articles.title: Palace seeks probe on Gracioso’s claims
articles.summary: Malacañang has called for a deeper probe into the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
Calire Castro

SINGAPORE – Malacañang has called for a deeper probe into the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members of her family on the instructions of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said evidence would show who is credible among those making conflicting claims.
She said Gracioso has shown that he was with the Vice President in some “personal” events.

“The investigation on this should be deeper, not for anyone but for the people because this involves public funds. Even if they claim that this is just politicking and that is their sole defense, those who are investigating this should not be stopped,” Castro said at a press briefing here.?
Duterte has denied Gracioso’s claims, saying the former policeman’s statements may have been motivated by money.
Velasco’s camp refuted the accusation, dismissing it as a “one-size-fits-all” narration “designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events.”
Meanwhile, Duterte’s camp lashed back at Castro over the latter’s statement that the Vice President knows alleged bagmen Ramil Madriaga and Gracioso.
“No one prevents anybody from playing dumb. But it’s embarrassing,” defense spokesman Michael Poa said. - Bella Cariaso

articles.title: COA upholds disallowance of P73.29 million OVP secret funds
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit has affirmed with finality the disallowance against the Office of the Vice President (OVP)’s P73.29 million in confidential funds that were spent in just 11 days in…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:00am
The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Audit has affirmed with finality the disallowance against the Office of the Vice President (OVP)’s P73.29 million in confidential funds that were spent in just 11 days in December 2022.

In a 15-page decision dated Oct. 5, the COA denied for lack of merit the motion for reconsideration filed by Vice President Sara Duterte, special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and OVP chief accountant Julieta Villadelrey.
It upheld its April 10 ruling that affirmed the notice of disallowance issued by the COA Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office on Aug. 8, 2024.
“The office has already anticipated the possibility of this decision and has prepared to respond through the appropriate legal and institutional channels,” the OVP said.
The OVP, however, said it has yet to receive a copy of the Oct. 5 COA resolution.
The notice covered expenses made from Dec. 21 to 31, 2022, from the total of P125-million confidential funds that the OVP received on Dec. 20 that year.
The disallowed amount included P69.787 million in rewards and P3.5 million in payments for tables, chairs, desktop computers and printers.
According to the notice, rewards were paid out as P10 million in cash, P34.857 million in various goods and P24.93 million in medicines.

The COA pointed out that the notice of disallowance was issued due to the failure of the OVP to submit documents showing the success of information-gathering and/or surveillance activities to support the payments of rewards to informers, as required by Joint Circular No. 2015-01 or the guidelines on the use of confidential and intelligence funds.
Instead, the COA said the OVP submitted a list of activities that the Vice President and officers of OVP satellite offices attended from Dec. 13 to 31, 2022.
Moreover, the list did not indicate or narrate the accomplishments that resulted from the information gathered or in the surveillance activities.
It also did not give weight to the OVP’s argument that the absence of untoward security-related incidents showed that it had complied with the requirement, saying such “does not hold water.”

The audit body also pointed out that the OVP submitted a certification from the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSG) listing routine security activities such as casing, liaising, surveillance, profiling and ocular inspections.

But the VPSG, as salaried personnel of the AFP, are “fundamentally disqualified” from receiving informer rewards under the joint circular, the COA said, and that submitting acknowledgement receipts for payments to salaried personnel, without proof of operational success from eligible non-employee informers, rendered the P69.787 million “completely unsubstantiated and disallowable in audit.” – Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Transgressive, edgy DIY: What the 90s meant for British art
articles.summary: The 1990s are remembered for Britpop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the…

image.caption: A new exhibition at Tate Britain takes viewers back to the 90s in BritainImage: Eddie Otchere

blocks.text: The 1990s in Britain are often remembered through a haze of n,ostalgia consisting of rave culture, Britpop and provocative art and fashion by the likes of Tracey Emin and Alexander McQueen.
Undeniably, the decade was a time of major change in British society — the long reign of Margaret Thatcher had come to an end and the West entered a period of relative post-Cold War stability.
Meanwhile, British cultural icons like Oasis, the Spice Girls and Vivienne Westwood garnered international fame.
But Tate Britain's new exhibition "The 90s: Art and Fashion," which opens on October 8 and runs through February 14, 2027, urges viewers to look beyond the familiar names and images.

Even though now prominent artists such as Damien Hirst and Juergen Teller are among the show's 70 contributors, the exhibition also aims to highlight the creative input of those in communities which were left out of the mainstream discourse.

After all, says chief curator Edward Enninful in the exhibition's program, "the energy of the 90s was not concentrated in a single movement, but distributed across communities, disciplines and geographies that have not always been equally represented."

blocks.caption: Fashion editor and style icon Edward Enninful curated the exhibitionImage: Adama Jalloh

blocks.text: An inclusive perspective

For Enninful, the exhibition is personal: The Ghanaian-born British fashion editor, stylist and creative director became the youngest-ever fashion director of i-D Magazine in the 90s at age 18, helping shape the diverse and experimental London fashion scene of the 1990s. He later became editor-in-chief of British Vogue in 2017.

Enninful writes that he and his co-curators aimed to present a body of work which "reflects a broader landscape of practices and voices that shaped the period, many of which operated beyond the structures of visibility at the time." The exhibition pays special attention to artists of color and women whose work was not necessarily showcased as prominently at the time.

Black masculinity became "a site of cultural negotiation" in Britain in the 90s, writes co-curator Helen Little in the program text: "Figures such as Chris Ofili, Steve McQueen, Keith Piper, Koto Bolofo and Ozwald Boateng reimagined the Black masculine, challenging the racist specter of Black men, who had been defined as part of a masculinity crisis linked to post-industrial decline and excluded from the narrative of 'Cool Britannia.'"
Just like "Swinging London" in the 1960s, "Cool Britannia" became a widespread phrase to refer to the 1990s as an era during which British youth culture, pop music, art and political optimism boomed.

blocks.caption: British-Ghanaian/Dominican photographer Eileen Perrier featured women of color who were rarely celebrated at the timeImage: Eileen Perrier/DACS

blocks.text: DIY meets Dr. Martens

The 90s also offered artists plenty of chances to create without waiting for support from traditional gatekeepers. Britain entered the decade in recession, but that economic uncertainty also left artists free to do what they wished.

Empty buildings and industrial spaces were turned into informal venues. A 23-year-old Damien Hirst orchestrated "Freeze," a self-organized student exhibition in 1988 in a disused London warehouse. It became a landmark early art exhibition for the generation of artists known as the "Young British Artists" or YBA.

Artists Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin opened The Shop, a temporary art gallery and social space in 1992, as a place where exhibitions could develop outside established galleries. Lucas and Emin also paved the way for women artists thanks to their deeply personal works and their edgy expressions of female liberation.

While the Spice Girls helped make feminism accessible to a younger generation of Brits in the 90s by popularizing the "girl power" slogan and shaping "identity through agency power and resistance," as argues Tate curator Helen Little, Emin and Lucas meanwhile "presented a new visual language of clothing as art to tackle societal taboos around female sexuality, vulnerability and desire" — from t-shirts with provocative slogans to a grunge look of scuffed Dr. Martens boots with razor blades. Their work "held a mirror up to gender, behavior and identity," Little writes.

blocks.caption: Sarah Lucas broke away from feminine ideals in raw works such as this 1997 photo titled 'Chicken Knickers'Image: Sarah Lucas/Sadie Coles HQ

blocks.text: Fashion and haute couture in the spotlight
At the same time, the British fashion industry came into the international spotlight.

In a feminine sensuality counter to the gender stereotypes dismissed by Emin and Lucas, waif-like Kate Moss came to represent the feminine ideal of the 1990s. Dubbed "heroin-chic," the style was an antithesis to the glamorous, athletic physiques of the supermodels who preceded her. Corinne Day's photographs of the model led to the raw aesthetic to be labelled "grunge" after the anguished style of rock music hailing from Seattle and led by Nirvana.

The trend has faced a significant cultural reexamination since: "Along with the look also came criticism that the strung-out look of drug or alcohol addiction was glamorized while encouraging serious eating disorders in a generation of young women," points out Alex Farquharson, director of the Tate Gallery in his foreword to the exhibition.

blocks.caption: The new Tate Britain exhibition includes photos of 90s icon Kate MossImage: Juergen Teller

blocks.text: The 1990s were also an exciting era for Britain in haute couture, as legendary designers John Galliano led Diorwhile Alexander McQueen started directing Givenchy at the age of 27.

McQueen's runway presentations were more akin to performance art than commercial fashion shows — and they often included historical critiques. Among them was the famous finale of his Fall/Winter 1998 collection at a London warehouse, during which the model stood in a circle of flames. Titled "Joan," the show was a reference to the killing of Joan of Arc.

McQueen designed several other runway shows that reflected on British history, with topics of conquest and punishment repeatedly coming to the forefront. His 1995 presentation "Highland Rape" referenced the history of Scotland's subjugation, with the designer describing it as "England's rape of Scotland."

blocks.caption: McQueen's fashion shows were more like performance art and included historical critiques of BritainImage: Guy Marineau/Vogue/Condé Nast

blocks.text: As co-curator Jessica Vaughan points out in her exhibition text: "Art, fashion and photography were not simply transgressive reactions … but reflected a genuine public unease with Britain's global identity and its past."

In a world that can now feel increasingly mediated by screens, algorithms and established platforms, the artwork of the 90s offers a reminder of the value of physical spaces and fresh DIY creativity of the last smartphone-free decade.

articles.title: Germany news: Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers
articles.summary: Political extremism threatens Germany's existing social order, Chancellor Merz has said. The Transport Ministry has proposed a five-year plan to improve Germany's ailing railroad infrastructure. DW…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026last updated October 7, 2026
Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers in own ranks

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday addressed the threat of political extremism to the existing social order, accusing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and far-left BSW parties of wanting to wipe out "the DNA of our democracy."
"Extremism," said Merz, "is forcing its way into our state legislatures with a vengeance."

Merz, speaking in Berlin, called this week’s election of an AfD politician as speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament — the first time a far-right politician has been tapped to lead a statehouse since 1945 — a "historic break."
Moreover, Merz slammed politicians — potentially from his own conservative CDU party — for casting ballots in favor of Tobias Rausch in the Saxony-Anhalt vote.
Rausch received 48 votes but the AfD and BSW only have 44 between them. It is unclear from whom Rausch picked up four extra votes — he was elected in a secret ballot.

Observers assume these came from within the CDU, but Merz said "false flag" attacks also occur in politics, implying the Social Democrats, the Left party and the Greens, all of which are also represented in the state's parliament, could be attempting to weaken or sow division in the CDU.
"Anyone ‌who ​casts their vote for the AfD is ​playing the extremists' game and undermining ⁠credibility," ​said Merz. "In any ‌case, this is incompatible ​with ⁠the values of my party, ⁠the ​CDU."

articles.title: EU enlargement: European Commission tables reforms to prepare bloc for new members
articles.summary: The European Commission is proposing earlier access to EU markets for candidate countries, new voting rules to reduce vetoes and extra safeguards for a bigger bloc. But is the reform fair — or even…

image.caption: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos presented the results of the bloc's pre-enlargement policy review on Tuesday: 'Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement,' she saidImage: Romeo Boetzle/EU

blocks.text: The European Commission wants to inject new momentum into its enlargement process, which has seen some candidate countries waiting for decades to join.
Albania, Montenegro, Moldova and Ukraine are currently the frontrunners to join the bloc, with EU officials expressing the hope that Montenegro could do so as early as 2028.
"A larger union is a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told journalists in Strasbourg on October 6.
One key question is how the EU can take in more countries in the near future without becoming harder to run or running the risk of democratic backsliding in new member states.

The Commission's answer to this question is to simultaneously require candidate countries to meet EU standards and get the bloc itself to reform by removing obstacles in the accession process and protecting its democratic values.
Less unanimity, more qualified majority votes

One of the main stumbling blocks in accession negotiations so far has been the need for unanimous decisions across all 27 members. In the past, individual states have often blocked a candidate's progress because of bilateral issues.
The delays caused by Hungary's blocking of Ukraine's negotiation process are a prominent example.

blocks.caption: EU officials hope that Montenegro could join the union as early as 2028. Pictured here: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (left) shakes hands with Montenegro's Prime Minister Milojko SpajicImage: Risto Bozovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Now — and not for the first time — the Commission is recommending that member states move away from the principle of unanimity for decisions like the opening of negotiation clusters, replacing it with qualified majority voting.
The unanimity dilemma

"Every cluster that you open is subject to three individual decisions, and every single decision is subject to unanimity. It's mind-blowing, and I think this clearly needs to go," a Commission official, who wished to remain anonymous, told journalists on Tuesday.
The catch is that a shift to qualified majority voting would itself require a unanimous decision.

"I have some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting," Tinatin Akhvlediani, head of the enlargement program at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS) told DW, pointing to previous attempts to change voting rules that were shot down by member states.
Gradual access to membership benefits

To incentivize reform in candidate countries, the Commission is proposing gradual integration, which means that these countries could be granted some of the benefits of membership before joining — as long as they meet the EU's criteria.

blocks.caption: Tinatin Akhvlediani of the Centre for European Policy Studies told DW that she had 'some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting'Image: privat

blocks.text: "Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement," Kos said on Tuesday, underlining that the process would stay merit-based.

This could have a motivational effect on candidate countries, Nina Vujanovic, a research fellow at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told DW: "Reforms are important, but it is also important to reward that process a little bit earlier, ahead of accession," she said.
Earlier access to EU benefits is not entirely new: Montenegro, for example, already participates in the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) even though it is not yet a member.
Addressing geopolitical realities
The Commission now wants to give candidate countries such early access more systematically and link it to strategic alignment.
"This is not something that will be available [to candidate countries] unless they really orient themselves on the EU," a Commission official told journalists.
Making strategic alignment a condition is new and reflects the EU's efforts to adjust to the geopolitical tensions members and candidates are facing.
Candidates' choice: Russia or the EU?

"The EU is trying to keep candidate countries out of the hands of Russia," Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at Bruegel, told DW. "Strategic alignment is aimed very squarely at politicians like Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, who has clearly promoted Russian interests," she said.

The new procedures would demand alignment not only with the EU's foreign and security policy, but also with its standards on economic security. "Trading gas with Russia is simply not something that builds trust with the European Union," said Nina Vujanovic.
The lessons the EU learned from Hungary, Poland

To prevent breaches of democratic rules by new member states, the Commission proposes a 15-year period within which it would be easier to sanction new members by cutting financial support or restricting voting rights.

blocks.caption: The foreign ministers of the 16 countries involved in the Berlin Process (the six candidate countries of the Western Balkans and 10 other European countries) met in Montenegro last weekImage: Regierung von Montenegro

blocks.text: In an interview with The Guardian and other European media, Commissioner Kos made it clear that the EU had learned its lesson from the democratic backsliding it saw in the past in countries like Poland or Hungary: "No more Viktor Orban. We have to have quicker mechanisms than only Article 7."
Double standard or necessary protection?
Critics point out that this safeguard would create unequal conditions within the union.
"It is inherently unfair," says Heather Grabbe. "In the 2040s, why should Montenegro face different conditions to, say, Slovenia?"

Many current candidate countries have a shaky record when it comes to democratic norms, as Tinatin Akhvlediani points out: "They are actually fragile democracies. So, this approach vis-a-vis these countries can be very much justified."

Experts say that while it might be desirable to apply similarly strict rules to all members, it is not realistically feasible as it would have to be approved unanimously and, as Grabbe says, "it's very hard to get turkeys to vote for Christmas."
Although the Commission's push for new rules in relation to enlargement is likely to move the debate forward, it is ultimately up to member states to decide how much of it becomes reality.

The European Council, which is made up of the heads of state or government of the 27 EU member states, the European Council president and the president of the European Commission, is expected to discuss the proposals at its upcoming meeting on October 15–16.
The outcome of those talks will determine how quickly the Commission's new enlargement agenda can move forward.

articles.title: Abortion pill access jumps almost 50% after Australia eases restrictions for pharmacies
articles.summary:
The number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023

  • Get our

blocks.text: The number of Australian pharmacies stocking an abortion pill increased by almost 50% when prescribing restrictions were relaxed, with researchers saying the findings suggest deregulation of abortion promotes safer and faster healthcare.

A study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open on Thursday examined the impact of changes by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 which meant the medication, MS-2 Step, could be prescribed by any GP.

Prior to the changes, GPs needed additional training and registration to prescribe it. The requirement for pharmacists to be registered to dispense the drug was also scrapped, and administrative hurdles were relaxed. Appropriately trained nurse practitioners and endorsed midwives also became eligible prescribers.

By comparing pharmacy ordering data in the two years before and after the changes, researchers led by La Trobe University found by mid-2025, 49% more pharmacies were stocking the medication. There were 2,228 pharmacies stocking it before the policy change, rising to 4,107 by mid-2025.

The number of postcodes with a pharmacy stocking the medication rose from 915 to 1,292 – or nearly half of all Australian postcodes – two years after the changes. Regional coverage increased from 23% to 35% of postcodes, while the proportion of stocking pharmacies in remote areas nearly doubled, rising from 12.5% to 22%.

The lead author of the paper, Prof Kristina Edvardsson from La Trobe University’s school of nursing and midwifery, said it showed “Australian women who need access to this medication can access it closer to home”.

“It removes the unnecessary travel and stress around getting the medication once it’s prescribed. That’s super important, particularly for women who might be more disadvantaged, women living in rural, remote areas, and women who might not have the means to travel.
“If you can go to your local pharmacy and pick up this medication, it means getting care quicker.”
Edvardsson said other studies have found improving access to MS-2 Step is safe, and that when access to the medical abortion pill increases, the need for surgical abortion decreases.

“In some European countries, medical abortion accounts for more than 90% of all abortions, and it looks like we’re heading that way here as well with a steady increase in medication abortion versus surgical abortion,” she said.
MS-2 Step, available under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, comprises two drugs used together, mifepristone and misoprostol. It can be taken until up to 63 days of gestation.
after newsletter promotion
At the time of the study, MS-2 Step was the only abortion pill available, but in February an additional drug, Arzestra, comprising the same two medicines, was approved by the TGA.

Dr Anna Noonan, a postdoctoral research fellow and abortion researcher with the University of Technology Sydney, said the data should be “an important signal” to countries where more restricted prescribing was still in place, such as the US.
“There are still pervasive, unnecessary barriers in lots of places, and data like this is an important signal that regulation and overregulation is not the way forward,” she said.

Noonan said there was still work to be done to improve rural and regional access, and that her own research suggested a lot of “invisible work” also occurred by local doctors, nurses and advocates working behind the scenes so that people can confidentially and more easily find healthcare.
“Doctors and nurses are going to pharmacies in advance saying, ‘I’m going to be an abortion provider in this community, will you stock this medication?’

“Overregulation creates extra work for those trying to provide timely care, and it doesn’t work out in the best interests of people seeking care,” Noonan said. “The more we encourage a deregulated environment, the easier access will be, particularly for people with less resources.”

articles.title: ‘Catastrophic wildfire loop’ after colonisation left parts of Australia more at risk from bushfires, study finds
articles.summary: Researchers found the shift from open woodland to dense forest after 1788 led to more intense fires, consistent with loss of cultural burning practices

blocks.text: The drastic land use changes wreaked by colonisation created a “catastrophic wildfire loop” that rendered south-east Australia more susceptible to climate-fuelled bushfires, experts say.

A team of researchers, working with the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, an organisation that represents traditional owners, reconstructed 1,000 years of vegetation and fire history at Purghagoolah, a lake surrounded by forest in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland, Victoria.

They analysed pollen and charcoal particles deposited over time in a metre-long sediment core, uncovering historical changes in the landscape and the interactions between weather, eucalypt cover and fire frequency and intensity.

blocks.caption: Aerial view of Purghagoolah (Lake Elusive) in Croajingolong national park in Gippsland, Victoria. Photograph: Michael-Shawn Fletcher

blocks.text: The results, published in Nature, revealed the shift from open woodland to dense forest after colonisation led to more intense fires, changes consistent with the loss of cultural burning practices and the removal of traditional owners, the Gunaikurnai people, from the land.
Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the University of Melbourne and the study’s lead author, said prior to colonisation “this was a cared for and managed landscape”.

“Gunaikurnai are removed from Country and you see a change in the amount of trees and shrubs in the landscape, and that drives more fires,” he said. “It’s actually land use change, more than a century before climate changes, that has allowed shrubs to increase, fires to get hotter. Those hot fires then trigger eucalypt recruitment. And the eucalypts then increase, driving further fire.”
Fletcher said the research provided scientific evidence for the value of cultural burning, and the importance of integrating Indigenous knowledge into modern fire management strategies.

blocks.caption: The field research team carries equipment through Croajingolong national park. Photograph: Michael-Shawn Fletcher

blocks.text: Cultural burning refers to the way First Nations people use low-temperature fire to maintain a safe and productive landscape. These practices, which are still used in parts of Australia today, are based on a responsive “right time, right place” approach that differs from mainstream prescribed burning practices undertaken by government agencies for hazard reduction.
“Hopefully this opens a conversation around the possibilities, into a new future where we can actually start getting control of the catastrophic fire problem,” Fletcher said.
after newsletter promotion

Prof David Bowman, a fire scientist based at the University of Tasmania, who was not an author of the paper, said the research was significant and contributed to the “growing realisation” about the legacy of landscape change resulting from the loss of Indigenous fire management.

“Other factors have exacerbated these changes, [such as] the introduction of non-native animals, non-native plants in some cases. These are very complex ecological processes, but taking out traditional fire management is a very significant thing to have happened.”

The long-term records were “critically important” for piecing together the historical changes in fire regimes, and how they’re responding to climate drivers, he said. “One of the big questions in wildfire science is how anomalous, or how unprecedented, is the stuff that’s happening?”
Bowman described the research as “like a pipe opener”. “I really hope that it opens up a conversation that we really need to have about managing our landscapes as the fire crisis is worsening.”

articles.title: Why music in Iran is more than just entertainment
articles.summary: Iranian authorities are trying to persuade prominent singers in exile to return home. While the state seeks to harness music as a political tool, music has also become a powerful expression of…

image.caption: Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, there has been an ongoing conflict between the Iranian state and musicImage: Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: After spending 47 years abroad, Iranian musician Bijan Mortazavi returned to his homeland at the end of September.
Mortazavi is one of Iran's most renowned violinists, singers, and composers.
In July 2026, he performed with his famous white violin at the closing ceremony of the FIFA World Cup alongside the New York Philharmonic Orchestra.

In the videos that he and his wife have now posted on social media, the couple can be seen taking walks through the city of the Iranian capital, Tehran, while passersby greet the musician warmly and welcome him.
Singer Mohsen Namjoo also recently returned to Iran after about 20 years in exile.
Internationally renowned for his experimental Persian music, he blends traditional Persian singing and poetic lyrics with elements of blues, rock, jazz, and folk.
In 2009, Namjoo was sentenced in absentia by a court in Tehran to five years in prison.
He was accused of insulting holy sites and mocking verses from the Quran, among other things.
In a video posted online after his return to Iran, Namjoo said he had returned to the country to spend more time with his family and friends.

blocks.caption: Women are prohibited from singing solo in Ira, but many young female musicians play and sing on the street without headscarves, defying the existing banImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Return as a political tool

On August 27, Abbas Salehi, Iran's minister of culture and Islamic guidance, said in an interview with the prominent Iranian media outlet Farhikhtegan that his ministry had compiled a list containing the names of more than 100 distinguished Iranians living abroad.
The goal, he said, was to remove obstacles to their travel or return to Iran.

Salehi stressed that even "critics of the Islamic Republic" could return at any time. He added, however, that the return of artists does not necessarily mean they would perform in Iran. Instead, they could simply visit the country, the minister said.
Sina Yousefi, a human rights lawyer, pointed to international law, specifically Article 12 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Iran is also a signatory.
According to this provision, no one may be arbitrarily prevented from entering their own country. This right cannot be made contingent on a citizen's level of loyalty to the government, he told DW.

"The idea of seeking out certain well-known figures — who the reformists, in particular, believe are less likely to cross the red lines — and winning them over to collaborate or bringing them back to the country is not new," said Sepideh Raissadat , an ethnomusicologist who has been studying the history and development of Persian music for years.

As an internationally renowned performer of classical Persian music, she combines her artistic work with scholarly research, with her dissertation focusing on the lives of Iranian female singers since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women
Between control and resistance

"The 1979 revolution in Iran was a revolution against music. Music was one of the red lines," said Raissadat, referring to statements by the leader of the revolution, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who as early as July 1979 had publicly described music as harmful to society and called for its complete abolition.

In a speech to employees of Radio Darya on July 21, 1979, Khomeini is said to have described music as "a betrayal of the country" and "a betrayal of the youth." A few days later, the Iranian newspaper Keyhan quoted him as saying that music was "like a drug” and must be completely eradicated.

During the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 to 1988, however, music made a comeback in the form of revolutionary and religious songs. It was also used to stir up feelings of national pride and a sense of belonging.

The regime also failed to completely banish the female voice from the public sphere. "They couldn't completely eliminate the voice of women. The female voice returned through choral singing," said Raissadat.
But the conflict between the state and music continued.

For years, musical instruments were not allowed to be shown on Iranian television. Instruments were confiscated or destroyed on the streets. Fearing repercussions, musicians did not carry their instruments in public, while some hid them in their cars.

"Listening to banned music at home was a political act. And when women began to sing, that, too, became a political act," Raissadat noted. The development of Iranian pop music was also part of this political and cultural tension, she underscored. "People began producing new domestic pop music to compete with music from Los Angeles."
Over the past ten years, social media — which is not entirely under government control — has become increasingly important and now wields considerable influence.
This change is particularly evident among young people, with young women now even playing the guitar without headscarves and performing in public.
Iranian singer finds voice in Germany
Music as an expression of protest
Raissadat observes a particular trend among the families of the young people who were killed during the nationwide mass protests in late December 2025 and January 2026.
The demonstrations began on December 28, 2025, and were violently suppressed by security forces.
Human rights organizations report that thousands of protesters were killed, but the exact figures are unknown due to the extensive information blackout imposed by the regime.

"The most important thing we've seen in recent years has been the use of music by the bereaved families of those killed in the protests. This stands in complete contrast to Shiite tradition and our history," said Raissadat.
At some funerals, families turned the memorial service for their loved ones into a new form of protest.
Instead of religious hymns, music played, and the mourners sang and danced along to it. In doing so, they created a deliberate contrast to traditional religious mourning rituals, the musician said.

"Music became a weapon. Those who were mourning were able to connect with it on their own, and at the same time, it stood in opposition to what the political system stands for," Raissadat pointed out, adding, "Dancing in white clothing also became an expression of this resistance."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
articles.summary:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new overseas Chinese…

blocks.text: Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new overseas Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.

Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.

The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.

The airport, about ⁠50km (30 miles) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken just months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.

Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.

The satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its September announcement, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.

blocks.caption: Construction under way at the site on 2 September. Photograph: Vantor/Reuters

blocks.text: Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.

Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.

After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.

US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.

After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while government of Laos has not commented on the project.

The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
The base would, however, give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes, it added.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?
articles.summary: The defense team also distances the Vice President from the insurance policies linked to her

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The defense team also distances the Vice President from the insurance policies linked to her

Amid the prosecution team’s attempt to prove the authenticity of bank accounts and insurance policies linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, the latter’s defense team had a strategy: distance the Vice President from these transactions.

Defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa wrote a letter to the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) to clarify matters about Duterte’s accounts with her father. Poa floated this letter during the impeachment trial on Wednesday, October 7, which was later read out loud by Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros during her interjection.
The letter was flashed on screen as Hontiveros read it out loud.

“Certain public statements have referred to purported bank accounts allegedly maintained with your institution bearing various account numbers hereto attached as Annex A. In light of these allegations and considering that our client has no knowledge, participation or recollection of maintaining or having any beneficial interest in such accounts, we respectfully request confirmation of the following,” the letter said, seeking clarification about the existence and status of the BPI accounts.
Poa addressed the letter to BPI senior vice president and legal counsel. Paul Rodrick Ysmael.

On Day 35 of the trial, BPI division head for central Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed that former president Rodrigo Duterte and daughter Sara had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million.

The account was opened in the BPI Julia Vargas branch in Pasig City, rolled over 12 times, and eventually reached P41.72 million. When the time deposit matured in March 2011, the funds were converted into a manager’s check.

Prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim explained that if funds were used to acquire a manager’s check, they will not reflect on the account’s year-end balance as they are considered “floating.” A manager’s check is valid for six months.

blocks.caption: Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution

blocks.text: So by saying that Duterte had no recollection of these accounts, did the defense say that this manager’s check transaction was all the idea of the former president?
“Well, to better phrase it your honor, our client, does not have any recollection of this account,” Poa told Hontiveros, who had the same question in mind.

The defense counsel added that his client only knew about the said bank account during the House quad committee hearings in 2024, which investigated Philippine offshore gaming operators, war on drugs, and illegal drugs.

“I was asked by the Vice President to verify kasi hindi niya natatandaan na may ganitong account at wala daw siyang transaksyon, ‘no (because she cannot remember that such an account exists and she is not aware of that transaction). So, in fact, that’s why we wanted to show even the response of the BPI to my letter,” Poa added.
But this was not the only thing that the Vice President is supposedly unaware of — or at least has no knowledge of.

During their cross-examination of witnesses from several insurance companies, the defense lawyers highlighted that the Vice President — although named in the policies — might not be directly involved in the transactions done by her husband.
For example, defense lawyer Carlo Joaquin Narvasa read to a witness section 3 of Republic Act No. 10607 or the law that amended the Insurance Code.

“The consent of the spouse is not necessary for the validity of an insurance policy taken out by a married person on his or her life or that of his or her children,” Narvasa said, reading the provision.
The consent of the spouse in insurance policies and other similar questions were repeated by defense counsels during the Wednesday trial. But for the prosecution, these excuses were unacceptable.
“Because, the SALN is a SALN. There are requirements for the SALN,” said prosecutor Terry Ridon.

“You have to ask your co-depositors, the co-joint accounts, whether that’s your spouse, your father, the content of these bank accounts before writing your SALN. That’s the process for all government officials preparing their SALN. So, hopefully, that’s what the Vice President should have done,” he added in Filipino.

What did the defense team — and the Vice President, for that matter — accomplish in claiming that Sara had no knowledge of the joint bank accounts with her father, who was detained in The Hague? Ridon had a response that mirrored the though balloon of many trial observers that day: “Magandang araw po, Pangulong Duterte. Nilalaglag po kayo rito.”
(Good morning, President Duterte. They’re throwing you under the bus here.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
articles.summary: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian rule
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, fuelling fears over a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.
Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president, Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised.

Last year, Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

But Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the 25 October run-off as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.
“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is called Flávio Bolsonaro as president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.

The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro raises hands with former presidential candidate Ronaldo Caiado (left) and Sao Paulo governor Tarcisio de Freitas during a rally in Goiania, Goias state, Brazil. Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Talíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”

Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”

Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multi-party democracy which the Sweden based V-Dem institute ranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.
But Jair Bolsonaro, who has praised authoritarian leaders including Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.

Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying to convince military chiefs to help him cling to power at the end of his 2018-2022 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the January 6 storming of the US Capitol.

Writing in the O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that, if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “the extreme and concrete danger of … another coup d’état attempt”.
“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote.

“If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration. Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him,” Leitão said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flash victory signs during a rally ahead of the presidential election runoff. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Political scientist Miguel Lago said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.

Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are also likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.
“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.

Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, including scrapping presidential term limits so he can seek indefinite re-election.

Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies, which have seen thousands jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years. Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.

On Tuesday, the president of Bolsonaro’s party, Valdemar Costa Neto, said that if Flávio Bolsonaro became president, he would release his father, who would then be “a strong candidate” in the 2030 presidential election.

articles.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors
articles.summary: Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
articles.byline: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem

blocks.text: The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs that it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.

The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London.

It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.

“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”
Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of countries like the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.

“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.
It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967, had seen its fair share of political upheaval.

The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.

But by the time the consul moved into, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before the new consul-general, John Henry Lewen, was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out, and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.

Lewen assumed his post at the present day consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position, as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.

As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”

Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war, and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.
Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah.

In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.

This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60-years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.
Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.
“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.

The Sandiganbayan has denied the bid of one of ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co’s co-accused in the flood control scam, a former official from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

According to a 24 Oras report on Wednesday, former DPWH official Juliet Calvo asked the Sandiganbayan Sixth Division if she could be under house arrest after suffering a stroke. The anti-graft court only allowed Calvo to remain in the Philippine Heart Center for 30 days.

The former DPWH official is facing a malversation charge in connection with an anomalous flood control project in Oriental Mindoro.
This is the same corruption case that Co is implicated in.

articles.title: South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
articles.summary: South Sudan's first general election is set for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts over whether the poll can be held credibly.
articles.byline: James Shimanyula, Eddy Micah Jr., Isaac Mugabi, Isaac Kaledzi

image.caption: South Sudan's President Salva Kiir is set to contest in the December electionImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22. It will be the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

But political tensions are high as preparations lag. Debate over the election intensified after President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.
Some voters are skeptical that the election will take place
Many are worried not only about the electoral logistics and insecurity in the country known for violent power struggles and political instability, according to Denis Logonyi, a Juba-based journalist.
Will elections happen in South Sudan?
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"People are having different views on these elections," Logonyi told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about elections," Logonyi told DW.
"There has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain," one voter said.
Another voter told DW that while South Sudanese are eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.
Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, the voter said.
Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline
Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.
On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue. Thirty-nine parties took part in discussions on the critical issues ahead of the election.
The meeting was initiated by Kiir, with some civil society groups left out, according to Logonyi. Minister of Cabinet Affairs Dr. Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges.

"Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted," Lomuro said.

"A credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."

According to Albino Akol Atak, the Deputy Rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline.
"The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear. We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles," Atak said.
Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, Secretary General of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said the success of the election would depend entirely on urgent, comprehensive collaboration.

"The South Sudan Opposition Alliance strongly believes that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders," Reath said.

"Given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."
Sudan has a history of planning then postponing elections
South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.

Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals — including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off since.
Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.
"The absence of Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."

The 2018 power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country. However, tensions between the two persisted.
In March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest and later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.

blocks.caption: South Sudan's former Vice President Riek Machar pictured in court in Juba in September 2025Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP

blocks.text: Key conditions envisioned for elections under peace deal not fulfilled yet

"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."

The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."
Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal are unfinished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.
Analysts have long been warning that the legitimacy of any election without these key issues being addressed would be undermined.

"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."
According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.
How instability persists in South Sudan
Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote
South Sudan is facing severe flooding, displacement and food insecurity. These conditions could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.
For communities displaced by conflicts in particular, there's uncertainty over how they would register and cast their ballots.
Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan
Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict.
Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process.
Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.
For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability.

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has appointed three new Court of Appeals (CA) Associate Judges — one of them being the daughter of former Executive Secretary Lucas Bersamin’s daughter, according to the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) on Wednesday.

articles.title: China's Golden Week reveals cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
articles.summary: Chinese visitors are returning from trips after the 13-day Golden Week holiday. Their subdued spending has raised fresh questions about domestic demand in the world's second-largest economy.

image.caption: Golden Week is typically a time of high levels of travel and spending in ChinaImage: Ryohei Moriya/The Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ya Xi just returned to Shanghai on a red-eye flight after her Golden Week trip to Southeast Asia. "I can stay up all night for a cheaper ticket," she told DW.
She was among the 31.19 million passengers who traveled during the 13-day holiday period that followed the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 25 and China's National Day on October 1.
Many of them spent their budgets more cautiously this year.

"I earn less this year, so I'm lowering my budget for this year's Golden Week," said Xi, who is in her mid-20s. "I spent 5,000 yuan (about €660) on my flight, which was the largest expense of my trip."

Golden Week is viewed as a barometer of the Chinese economy with Beijing using it as an opportunity to showcase the world's second-largest economy's spending power. State media, for instance, reported a record-breaking 25.204 million passenger trips on China's railway network on October 1.

blocks.caption: State media reported record-breaking train passenger numbers over Golden WeekImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, early data indicated more moderate spending per traveler and broadly flat passenger traffic, according to Citigroup analysts. Traffic volume during the first four days of the holiday rose just 0.1% year over year, far below the 3.5% increase seen during this year's Labor Day vacation.
Selective spending among younger consumers
Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese Economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told DW that Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly selective.
"My read is that people are willing to get out and spend. They're just being much more careful about how much and what they spend on," Lee said.

But being cautious doesn't mean staying frozen, she added. "They'll spend on travel, concerts, restaurants, experiences, and tech… if they think it's worth it, they'll economize pretty aggressively elsewhere."

Xi's Golden Week trip followed this pattern, paying more for significant experiences and economizing elsewhere: "Eat, drink, and be merry," said Xi, indicating she was willing to spend more on food. For example, she set a 200-yuan (about €26) budget for each meal.

blocks.caption: Many Chinese are opting for budget travel options instead of luxury tripsImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Guo-Chen Wang, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told DW that the budget-travel trend among Chinese visitors was ongoing.
"The number of trips is increasing, butconsumption remains strained, as I saw in past years," Wang said.

The Chinese government attempted to boost Golden Week spending by providing coupons worth more than 310 million yuan (€41.2 million). Wang remained unconvinced about the effectiveness of such a measure: "That's an old solution to an old problem."
A sign of China's weak domestic demand

It isn't the first Golden Week to see weak consumer demand. During last year's holiday season, the average spending per trip was 911.04 yuan (around €121), the lowest in three years, according to Reuters.
"Beijing still believes the low spending was due to consumers' reluctance [to spend]," Wang said. "In fact, we think Chinese consumers are unable to spend."

While savings kept increasing in Chinese banks, Wang said the vast majority of the savings are held by a small proportion of the population. "In other words, the majority of Chinese people don't have savings."
"The fundamental issue is the wealth gap in Chinese society," he said. "I don't know whether Beijing really neglected this problem or was simply unwilling to face it."
China’s tourism surge: expansion, regulation and challenges

A recent International Monetary Fund publication, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, once again noted that China's domestic demand has been weak since the pandemic, when the property market correction began.
Lee, however, saw weak spending during this Golden Week as a confidence problem.

"Theproperty downturnhas hit household wealth, income and job expectations are still pretty soft, and several years of weak prices have trained people to wait for discounts and hunt for value," she told DW.
Tightened cross-border rules played a limited role

Weeks before the Golden Week, China's tightened travel restrictions took effect on September 15. The new restrictions ban citizens from leaving the country if they are deemed to pose a risk to national as well as industrial or technological security.

Wang expected Chinese tourists to turn to domestic travel under the new rules, but the outcome did not match his expectations. "The volume of travel abroad is in fact growing, though not by much," he said.
Lee said she saw little evidence of a broad chilling effect on ordinary outbound tourism, with the Golden Week numbers serving as a "useful reality check."
"The September rules give authorities more room to verify travel purposes and ask for additional information in some cases," Lee said. "They still leave plenty of room for ordinary overseas tourism."
Mi Tang in Taipei contributed to this article.

articles.title: Over 20 Chinese ships spotted in Palawan waters on Wednesday, October 7, 2026 -- PCG
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) observed that there were more than 20 Chinese vessels spotted in the vicinity waters of Pag-asa Island, Palawan on Wednesday, GMA News' Ivan Mayrina reported in "24…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 9:15pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) observed that there were more than 20 Chinese vessels spotted in the vicinity waters of Pag-asa Island, Palawan on Wednesday, GMA News' Ivan Mayrina reported in "24 Oras."
The ships that are from the Chinese Maritime Militia and the Chinese Coast Guard were hovering in the island’s waters.
The PCG said they observed that there were more ships earlier and that some already left Pag-asa Island’s waters.
Last month, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), there have been more than 100 Chinese ships recorded within the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

“Month of September, we monitored 101 different vessels ng Coast Guard at ng PLA (People’s Liberation Army) Navy. Ito naman, if we look at it over a longer period of time, let's say six month period kagaya ng first sem assessment natin, na dumami ang kanilang Coast Guard vessels...based on their posture, they will be focusing on enforcing maritime law, 'yung maling pananaw niya sa maritime law, utilizing 'yung China Coast Guard ships para i-push nila ang kanilang mandato,” AFP spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said.

(For the month of September, we monitored 101 different vessels of the Coast Guard and of the PLA Navy. Here, if we look at it over a longer period of time, let's say six month period of the first semester assessment, there have been more Coast Guard vessels… based on their posture, they will be focusing on enforcing maritime law, their wrong view of the maritime law, utilizing the Chinese Coast Guard ships to push their mandate.)
Pag-asa Island is a hotspot for these Chinese ships, together with Escoda Shoal and Bajo de Masinloc.
Last week, Chinese Coast Guard vessels blocked Philippine officials from responding to a Chinese fishing vessel performing illegal dynamite fishing at the Sandy Cay near Pag-asa Island.
Meanwhile, PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan led the activation of the Coast Guard Auxiliary District in the Kalayaan Island District on Wednesday.
Gavan said that these citizens have an important role in overseeing the country’s sovereignty.
“Hindi tayo nahihinaan ng loob. We will match them hangga't kaya natin. Ship for ship, patrol for patrol. 'Yung mga maling naratibo nila, kino-correct natin sa tamang naratibo,” Trinidad said.
(Our resolve will not weaken. We will match them as much as we can. Ship for ship, patrol for patrol. Their wrong narratives, we will correct it with the right ones.) — Jean Mangaluz/BAP, GMA News
